title: Creating a figure
text:
1 The Makie visualization ecosystem







TipOn the name: Makie



The name “Makie” is derived from the Japanese word, 蒔絵 (*Maki-e”), which translates literally to “sprinkled picture”.

The name Makie (we pronounce it Mah-kee) is derived from the japanese word Maki-e, which is a technique to sprinkle lacquer with gold and silver powder. Data is the gold and silver of our age, so let’s spread it out beautifully on the screen!
— Makie README



1.1 What is Makie?
Makie is a visualization framework for Julia. It provides abstractions (types and functions) to compose 2D and 3D static, interactive, and animated figures. Makie’s abstractions support higher level geometric and data visualization semantics for us to express and communicate our ideas, concepts, and data graphically, decoupled from the lower level software, operating system, and hardware computing stack that renders these semantics into display pixels or digital media files. That is, we can use Makie to compose our figure in terms of the fundamental Euclidean geometries (points, lines, polygons etc.) or higher-order data-centric plots (scatter plots, line plots, histograms, etc.), while a Makie backend will convert our figure composition into pixels, vector graphics, or an interactive display.


1.2 Installing Makie
We typically do not install Makie directly, but rather install (and use) a particular Makie backend, such as CairoMakie, GLMakie, or WGLMakie. A Makie backend is the infrastructure that handles translating our ideas, thoughts, concepts, and data expressed in terms of geometries, statistical plots, aesthetics (color, styling), and so on into instructions that will result in our composition being rendered to a display or a file. We need to provision a Julia environment with a Makie backend for Makie to be available to Julia programs running in that environment. We do this by installing the Makie backend package into the environment using the standard Julia package management system. In this series, we will be using the GLMakie backend, as it is more REPL-flow friendly and also to take advantage of Makie’s interactivity features when we need to.
using Pkg
Pkg.add("GLMakie")
As with all package installations, we only need to do this once for any particular backend and any particular environment.


1.3 Loading and activating a backend
To have the Makie abstractions and functionality available to Julia programs and other packages that depend on them in a particular environment, we typically load a particular backend, which re-exports (or implements) the Makie interface, rather than the Makie package directly:
using GLMakie
Note that When using packages from the broader Makie ecosystem, we have to explicitly load the backend we want to use for the other packages to work.
For example:
using GLMakie
using PhyloMakie
using PhyloPicMakie
using GeoMakie

title: Creating a figure
text:
2 Composing a Makie Figure
We use Makie to express and communicate visual concepts by building them up in a series of nested layers: A Figure instance tracks a collection of Axis instances, each of which tracks a collection of Plot instances.
A typical Makie visualization looks like:

# Set up the figure
fig = Figure()

# Set up the plotting frame
ax = Axis(fig[x, y]; ...)

# Create the plots
plotting_function1!(ax, ....)
plotting_function2!(ax, ....)
...

# Display/save plot
....

2.1 The Figure type
A Makie composition starts by creating a new Figure instance:

figure1 = Figure()








We use instances of the Makie Figure type as the top-level container for our entire composition, to track the layout of one or more Axis instance The Figure type does not itself store any direct plotting data, but rather tracks layout data for one or more instances of the Axis type, each of each serves as a self-contained drawing region.



2.2 The Axis type
We create an Axis instance by passing its location within a Figure.

ax1 = Axis(figure1[1, 1])

Makie.Axis with 0 plots:


Each instance of the Axis type tracks a distnct collection of Plot instances, each of which, in turn represent one sets of plotting or drawing data.
A Figure organizes our composition into a grid, in which particular grid positions are referenced by [row, column] indexing. Here we are assigning our new Axis object into the first grid position of figure1: figure1[1, 1].
The Figure object creates space for the grid position as we refer to them, so, if we do not add any Axis into any other grid position, our figure1 will be a single grid cell with the ax1. One figure can contain several axes, and one axis can contain several plot objects. A plot object is one visual representation inside that composition.
As can be seen, our new Axis has 0 plots in it. An Axis can contain multiple plot objects, all positioned within its coordinate system. We build up the visual content of our composition by adding Plot objects to our Axis, ax1, just as we build up a drawing by adding marks and shapes to a canvas.


2.3 The Plot
Plot objects are collections of visual elements we place on our figurative canvas. A Plot object can represent something as simple as a single point, line, polygon, or something more complex such as a collections of points, lines, line segments, or histograms or surfaces.

title: Geospatial data visualization with GeoMakie.GeoAxis
text:
0.0.1 Geospatial data visualization: minimal working example

using GeoMakie, CairoMakie
1fig = Figure()
2ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1])
3lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines())
fig


1

Create a Figure object: container for the plots

2

Create a GeoAxis object in cell (1, 1) of the Figure container: a specialized plotting axis that maps points from various geographical coordinate reference into Cartesian plotting planar coordinate systems; fig[1, 1] assigns it to the cell (1, 1), which is the only cell in a single plot figure.

3

Use the lines! function to plot coastline data on the GeoAxis plotting axis.

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect from Julia
text:
1 Install EDirect
NCBI Entrez Direct (EDirect) provides programs for searching and retrieving records from the Entrez databases. EDirect requires a Unix-compatible shell. On Windows, use Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL).
Run the installer from the system shell:
$ sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/entrezdirect/install-edirect.sh)"
The $ marks the shell prompt and is not part of the command. The installer places EDirect in ~/edirect and offers to add that directory to PATH. Accept the offer, then restart the terminal if instructed.
Confirm that the shell finds each program used below:
$ command -v esearch epost efetch xtract
/home/student/edirect/esearch
/home/student/edirect/epost
/home/student/edirect/efetch
/home/student/edirect/xtract

$ esearch -version
26.2
The path contains the local user name. The version may be newer than the one shown here. The EDirect release notes document version changes.
Create a project directory and start Julia with a project environment:
$ mkdir -p bear-edirect-project
$ cd bear-edirect-project
$ julia --project=.
Add DataFrames.jl from Julia’s package mode:
julia> ]

pkg> add DataFrames
Press Backspace at an empty pkg> prompt to return to julia>.
Load the required names and create the raw-data directory:
julia> using DataFrames: DataFrame, leftjoin, nrow, select, unstack

julia> import Dates

julia> raw_dir = joinpath("data", "raw")
"data/raw"

julia> mkpath(raw_dir)
"data/raw"

julia> pwd()
"/home/student/bear-edirect-project"

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect from Julia
text:
2 Run external programs from Julia
Julia’s external-program interface represents a command as a value. Julia launches the program directly; it does not place a shell between Julia and the program.

2.1 Construct a command
Backticks construct a Cmd object without running it:
julia> version_command = `esearch -version`
`esearch -version`

julia> typeof(version_command)
Cmd

julia> collect(version_command)
2-element Vector{String}:
 "esearch"
 "-version"
Each element of the command is 1 program argument.


2.2 Run a command
run starts the program and leaves its standard output connected to the terminal:
julia> run(version_command);
26.2
A command that exits with a nonzero status causes run to throw a ProcessFailedException. The success function runs a command and reports its exit status as a Boolean:
julia> success(`esearch -version`)
true


2.3 Capture standard output
read runs the program and returns its complete standard output. A terminal newline remains part of the captured string:
julia> version_text = read(version_command, String)
"26.2\n"

julia> ncodeunits(version_text)
5
readchomp removes 1 trailing line ending:
julia> edirect_version = readchomp(version_command)
"26.2"


2.4 Interpolate arguments
$ interpolates Julia values into a Cmd. A string remains 1 argument even when it contains spaces or characters that a shell would interpret:
julia> organism_name = "Ailuropoda melanoleuca"
"Ailuropoda melanoleuca"

julia> organism_query = "\"$(organism_name)\"[Scientific Name]"
"\"Ailuropoda melanoleuca\"[Scientific Name]"

julia> search_command = `esearch -db taxonomy -query $organism_query`
`esearch -db taxonomy -query '"Ailuropoda melanoleuca"[Scientific Name]'`

julia> collect(search_command)
5-element Vector{String}:
 "esearch"
 "-db"
 "taxonomy"
 "-query"
 "\"Ailuropoda melanoleuca\"[Scientific Name]"
Interpolating a collection supplies several arguments:
julia> requested_fields = ["TaxId", "ScientificName", "Rank"];

julia> field_command = `xtract -pattern Taxon -element $requested_fields`
`xtract -pattern Taxon -element TaxId ScientificName Rank`
Shell operators such as | and > do not connect or redirect programs inside Julia backticks. Julia values, IOBuffer, read, write, and pipeline provide those operations.


2.5 Supply standard input
An IOBuffer presents a Julia string as an input stream. The following pipeline call attaches that stream to the standard input of exactly 1 external program:
julia> sample_xml = """
       <Rows>
         <Row><taxon>Ursidae</taxon><rank>family</rank></Row>
         <Row><taxon>Selachii</taxon><rank>superorder</rank></Row>
       </Rows>
       """;

julia> sample_tsv = read(
           pipeline(
               `xtract -pattern Row -element taxon rank`;
               stdin = IOBuffer(sample_xml),
           ),
           String,
       )
"Ursidae\tfamily\nSelachii\tsuperorder\n"
The external program receives sample_xml through standard input. Julia captures the program’s standard output in sample_tsv.


2.6 Save and read text
write stores the captured string and returns the number of bytes written:
julia> sample_path = joinpath(raw_dir, "xtract-example.tsv")
"data/raw/xtract-example.tsv"

julia> write(sample_path, sample_tsv)
35

julia> readlines(sample_path)
2-element Vector{String}:
 "Ursidae\tfamily"
 "Selachii\tsuperorder"
open can direct a program’s standard output to a file without first materializing that output as a String:
julia> open(joinpath(raw_dir, "xtract-example-direct.tsv"), "w") do output
           run(
               pipeline(
                   `xtract -pattern Row -element taxon rank`;
                   stdin = IOBuffer(sample_xml),
                   stdout = output,
               ),
           )
       end;
This form still invokes only 1 external program.

title: Acquiring molecular characters with EDirect from Julia
text:
4 Combine identifiers from multiple queries
Separate searches express a sampling design that names independent targets rather than 1 taxonomic subtree.

4.1 Save separate results and combine them
Specify 1 representative for each of 3 mammal orders:
julia> mammal_targets = DataFrame(
           order = ["Primates", "Rodentia", "Artiodactyla"],
           scientific_name = [
               "Homo sapiens",
               "Mus musculus",
               "Bos taurus",
           ],
           file_stem = ["primates", "rodents", "artiodactyls"],
       );

julia> mammal_queries = [
           "\"$(name)\"[Scientific Name]"
           for name in mammal_targets.scientific_name
       ];
Run each esearch invocation, then pass each captured result to a separate efetch invocation:
julia> mammal_search_results = [
           read(`esearch -db taxonomy -query $query`, String)
           for query in mammal_queries
       ];

julia> mammal_uid_texts = [
           read(
               pipeline(
                   `efetch -format uid`;
                   stdin = IOBuffer(search_xml),
               ),
               String,
           )
           for search_xml in mammal_search_results
       ];

julia> mammal_targets.taxid = parse.(Int, strip.(mammal_uid_texts));

julia> select(mammal_targets, :order, :scientific_name, :taxid)
3×3 DataFrame
 Row │ order          scientific_name  taxid
     │ String         String           Int64
─────┼────────────────────────────────────────
   1 │ Primates       Homo sapiens       9606
   2 │ Rodentia       Mus musculus      10090
   3 │ Artiodactyla   Bos taurus         9913
Write 1 identifier file per query:
julia> mammal_id_paths = [
           joinpath(raw_dir, "$(stem)-taxid.txt")
           for stem in mammal_targets.file_stem
       ];

julia> write.(mammal_id_paths, mammal_uid_texts);

julia> readlines.(mammal_id_paths)
3-element Vector{Vector{String}}:
 ["9606"]
 ["10090"]
 ["9913"]
Read the separate files, concatenate their rows, and write the combined file:
julia> combined_mammal_taxids = reduce(vcat, readlines.(mammal_id_paths))
3-element Vector{String}:
 "9606"
 "10090"
 "9913"

julia> write(
           joinpath(raw_dir, "mammal-representative-taxids.txt"),
           join(combined_mammal_taxids, '\n') * "\n",
       );


4.2 Append repeated query results
Open a fresh destination and append each captured efetch result to its IOStream:
julia> appended_path = joinpath(
           raw_dir,
           "mammal-representative-taxids-appended.txt",
       );

julia> open(appended_path, "w") do output
           for query in mammal_queries
               search_xml = read(
                   `esearch -db taxonomy -query $query`,
                   String,
               )
               uid_text = read(
                   pipeline(
                       `efetch -format uid`;
                       stdin = IOBuffer(search_xml),
                   ),
                   String,
               )
               write(output, uid_text)
           end
       end;

julia> @assert readlines(appended_path) == combined_mammal_taxids
Opening the destination with "w" replaces any previous content before the loop begins. Opening the file separately with "a" would retain old content and duplicate identifiers when the cell is rerun.

11 Interpret the data
bears-CYTB-raw.fasta contains 1 CYTB sequence for each of the 8 specified, non-extinct bear species returned by the Taxonomy query.

CYTB is 1 linked mitochondrial locus.
A mitochondrial gene tree can differ from the species history because of introgression, lineage sorting, sampling, and other processes.
One record per species does not represent within-species variation.
Database annotations and taxonomic assignments can change.
The raw FASTA sequences require alignment and alignment inspection before phylogenetic inference.

title: Adding images to phylogenies
text:
This tutorial develops 1 small analysis in the same order that we would work through it at the Julia REPL:
We will first confirm the tree topology and tip labels. We will then add 1 supplied image to each tip. No image discovery is required.

title: Adding images to phylogenies
text:
1 Load the plotting packages







NoteRequired packages



GLMakie and PhyloMakie.jl need to be installed in the active environment. If this has not already been done, run:
using Pkg

Pkg.add("GLMakie")
Pkg.add("PhyloMakie")

Load the packages with:
using GLMakie
using PhyloMakie

title: Adding images to phylogenies
section: 2 Store the phylogeny as a Newick string
text:
2 Store the phylogeny as a Newick string
The tip labels are the 7 colors red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. The nested parentheses describe a fully bifurcating ladderized tree.

phylogeny_newick = "(red,(orange,(yellow,(green,(blue,(indigo,violet))))));"

"(red,(orange,(yellow,(green,(blue,(indigo,violet))))));"


Read the parentheses from the inside out. indigo and violet are sister tips. Their clade is successively joined by blue, green, yellow, orange, and red.

title: Adding images to phylogenies
text:
3 Parse the Newick string

phylogeny = parsephylogeny(NewickFormat(), phylogeny_newick)

LineageNetwork(13 nodes, 12 edges, 7 tips, 0 hybrid nodes, rooted)


The variable phylogeny_newick contains text. The variable phylogeny contains the phylogeny object that PhyloMakie can plot.

title: Adding images to phylogenies
section: 4 Plot the tree before adding images
text:
4 Plot the tree before adding images

tree_result = plot(
    phylogeny;
    useedgelength = false,
    tipoffset = 0.12,
)

tree_result.figure







Figure 1: The ladderized phylogeny before tip images are added.





This first plot is a checkpoint. Before adding another layer, confirm that all 7 labels are present and that indigo and violet are sisters.

section: 5 Use the supplied Wikimedia Commons images
text:
5 Use the supplied Wikimedia Commons images

The dictionary below gives us direct PNG URLs that PhyloMakie can download and decode. The indigo and violet values request PNG previews of SVG source files.

image_urls = Dict(
    "red" => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7f/Red-ff0000.png",
    "orange" => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a8/Solid_orange.png",
    "yellow" => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6d/Solid_yellow.png",
    "green" => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c7/Solid_green.png",
    "blue" => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e5/Solid_blue.png",
    "indigo" => "https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Solid_indigo.svg/960px-Solid_indigo.svg.png",
    "violet" => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Solid_violet.svg/960px-Solid_violet.svg.png",
)

Dict{String, String} with 7 entries:
  "indigo" => "https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Solid_i…
  "yellow" => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6d/Solid_yellow…
  "orange" => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a8/Solid_orange…
  "blue"   => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e5/Solid_blue.p…
  "violet" => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Solid_…
  "green"  => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c7/Solid_green.…
  "red"    => "https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7f/Red-ff0000.p…


Every dictionary key exactly matches 1 tip label in phylogeny_newick. That exact match tells PhyloMakie which image belongs to which tip.







NoteInternet connection



PhyloMakie downloads these images when the illustrated tree is first plotted. The plotting step therefore requires an internet connection.

title: Adding images to phylogenies
text:
6 Describe the image annotations
ImageAnnotation controls where and how large an image appears. Tips are 1 data unit apart vertically, so an image height below 1 leaves space between adjacent images.

image_height = 0.65

tip_images = Dict(
    label => ImageAnnotation(
        url;
        position = :right,
        height = image_height,
    ) for (label, url) in image_urls
);

We now have 3 objects with separate jobs:







Object
Role




phylogeny
Stores the topology parsed from the Newick string.


image_urls
Maps each exact tip label to a supplied image URL.


tip_images
Adds placement and sizing instructions for each image.

title: Adding images to phylogenies
section: 7 Plot the images before moving the labels
text:
7 Plot the images before moving the labels
First, keep the small tipoffset from the original tree plot. This lets us see why image placement and text placement need to be adjusted separately.

close_labels_result = plot(
    phylogeny;
    nodeimages = tip_images,
    useedgelength = false,
    tipoffset = 0.12,
    xlim = (0.5, 9.0),
    ylim = (0.25, 7.75),
)

close_labels_result.figure







Figure 2: With the original tip-label offset, the labels begin inside the images.





Two arguments are doing different jobs:

position = :right places the left edge of each image at its tip node, so the image extends to the right of the tree.
tipoffset = 0.12 places each tip label only 0.12 x-axis data units to the right of its tip node.

The image and the label therefore occupy some of the same space. Changing position would move the image. To move only the text, change tipoffset.

title: Adding images to phylogenies
section: 8 Move the tip labels past the images
text:
8 Move the tip labels past the images
Increase tipoffset while leaving tip_images unchanged. The tree topology, image size, and image placement all remain the same.

illustrated_result = plot(
    phylogeny;
    nodeimages = tip_images,
    useedgelength = false,
    tipoffset = 0.9,
    xlim = (0.5, 9.0),
    ylim = (0.25, 7.75),
)

illustrated_result.figure







Figure 3: The ladderized phylogeny with a supplied color image mapped to each tip.





The nodeimages argument adds the image dictionary to the live tree plot. The larger tipoffset moves the tip-label text past the images, and the explicit axis limits reserve space for both the images and the labels.

title: Adding images to phylogenies
text:
9 REPL checkpoint
First change the final plot’s tipoffset from 0.9 to 1.2 and rerun that plotting cell. Only the text should move. Then change image_height from 0.65 to 0.45, rebuild tip_images, and rerun the plotting cell again. Only the image size should change on the second pass. The topology and the tip-image matches should stay the same.
If a tip has no image, compare its Newick label with the corresponding image_urls key. The 2 strings must match exactly.

title: Working with randomness and probabilities
text:
Proficiencies

Sampling a single random value of a specified numeric type (e.g., Int, Float64) using rand.
Sampling multiple random values of the specified type and length using rand.
Sampling uniformly from \((0, 1]\) using rand()
How to sample a vector of independent uniform random Float64 values in \((0, 1]\) by passing a length to rand.
How to sample a matrix of independent uniform random Float64 values in \((0, 1]\) by passing row and column dimensions to rand.
How to sample uniformly at random from a defined integer range using rand with a range argument (e.g., rand(-500:500, n)).
How to sample uniformly at random from an explicit collection of values (e.g., an array of floats or characters) using rand.












TipFunctions vs methods in Julia



In Julia, a function is a operation that can accept inputs and returns outputs. A function of a particular name (e.g. range, rand, my_custom_function) may have a number of different methods, or implementation that are distinguished by the pattern of arguments the function takes (called the signature of the function).
See: Julia: Functions, methods, and signatures

The rand function is the function we will most often use to generate random variates of different shapes, and sizes and characteristics. The rand function has a number of different methods, that is, different approaches for generating random values of various different data types, structures, and ranges, depending on the arguments passed to it.



The core Julia library provides rand methods that generate values by sampling them from ranges and collections under a uniform probability distribution. Packages such as Distributions.jl, covered separately, provide the ability to sample random values from a broader range of distributions.






TipProbability distributions











Sampling a random integer between its smallest and largest representible value with uniform random probability:
rand(Int) 
Sampling a random real (continuous or floating-point) value from across its 64-bit representation range with uniform random probability:

rand(Float64)

0.4974424583488273


Sampling a random character value from across its possible values with uniform random probability:

rand(Char)

'\Ude1cd': Unicode U+DE1CD (category Cn: Other, not assigned)





A vector of 10 i.i.d (identically and independently distributed) uniformly-distributed integers:

rand(Int, 10)

10-element Vector{Int64}:
 -1689897989651709639
 -6690054032961497285
  8927189725056694540
  3355313422696072122
  2408082346224331173
  1130349617041145176
  4449108396211924995
  7831571604185914584
 -4379413307566119193
  8579230336753964277


A vector of 10 i.i.d (identically and independently distributed) uniformly-distributed (64-bit) floating-point values:

rand(Float64, 10)

10-element Vector{Float64}:
 0.8033012459562863
 0.17010273370581364
 0.9676743700821571
 0.6447940191307234
 0.7985743231803294
 0.5697890493145663
 0.2508400432572976
 0.021631443906063974
 0.9056614898065614
 0.7291454219839901





Multidimensional collections of values can be generated by the syntax, rand(Type, n, m), where n is the number of rows and m the number of columns.
Sampling a \(2 \times 3\) matrix of random Int values:

rand(Int, 2, 3)

2×3 Matrix{Int64}:
 6265999629731388449  -8150425254198309967  7356714132623612319
 3024329044416745726  -2719808690514237401  -447595415291895092


Sampling a \(2 \times 3\) matrix of random Float64 values:

rand(Float64, 2, 3)

2×3 Matrix{Float64}:
 0.408631  0.19001   0.979878
 0.844747  0.517719  0.12903





We can use methods of the rand function that take range objects to constrain the values to particular ranges. Instead of a type (Int, Float64, and so on), we can pass the rand function a range object to sample with uniform probability from the intervals or collections of values represented by the range object.
Sampling 10 integer values from the closed interval [-5, 5] with uniform random probability:

rand(-5:5, 10)

10-element Vector{Int64}:
 -2
  5
 -2
  3
  5
 -4
 -3
  3
 -1
  5


Sampling 10 real values from the closed interval [-5.0, 5.0] (binned into 0.1 units) with uniform random probability:

rand(-5.0:0.1:5.0, 10)

10-element Vector{Float64}:
 -4.0
 -1.5
  1.4
 -4.3
 -0.4
  3.5
  3.7
  1.8
 -3.2
 -2.1






rand([0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4], 2)

2-element Vector{Float64}:
 0.4
 0.4



rand(['A', 'C', 'G', 'T'], 3)

3-element Vector{Char}:
 'G': ASCII/Unicode U+0047 (category Lu: Letter, uppercase)
 'A': ASCII/Unicode U+0041 (category Lu: Letter, uppercase)
 'C': ASCII/Unicode U+0043 (category Lu: Letter, uppercase)



rand(["Frodo", "Gandalf", "Eowyn", ], 4)

4-element Vector{String}:
 "Gandalf"
 "Frodo"
 "Gandalf"
 "Gandalf"





Note that while both produce identical results. In one, we use the range function (the 1:4 is short-hand for range(1, 4))
rand(1:4, , 10)
## Sample 10 values from the collection of values `[1, 2, 3, 4]`
rand([1, 2, 3, 4], 10) 



Sample a single random Float64 sampled uniformly from $(0, 1]`.
rand() 
Sample a vector of 5 independent uniform random values in \((0, 1]\).
rand(5)
Sample a \(2 \times 3\) matrix of independent uniform random values in \((0, 1]\).
julia> rand(2, 3)
2×3 Matrix{Float64}:
 0.731902  0.184771  0.992814
 0.442018  0.661203  0.107552




A uniform distribution between value \(a\) and \(b\), with support of continuous values in the real interval \([a, b]\) is denoted
\[
\mathcal{U}(a, b).
\]
A uniform distribution between value \(a\) and \(b\), with support of integer values in a finite set of integers in the interval \([a, b]\), is denoted
\[
\mathcal{U}(a, \dots, b).
\]



The hist function provides a variety of methods to visualize data in histogram formats.

using CairoMakie
data = rand(Float64, 1000)
hist(data)










Exercise 1
Generate \(N = 1000\) samples from each of the following distributions, and plot their histograms.

\(\mathcal{U}(-10, 10)\)
\(\mathcal{U}(-10, \dots, 10)\)

Advanced

Write a function, plot_uniform that takes three integer (Int) arguments, range_start, range_end, and n_samples, and plots the results.
Using this, produce plots of \(N \in \{1 \times 10^4, 1 \times 10^5, \}\) etc., to see how the histograms appear more and more uniform as the sample size increases.







Exercise 2We previously used range to generate a regular grid of value for one set of coordinates:

α = 0.5
z_vals = range(0.0, 1/α; length = 400)

0.0:0.005012531328320802:2.0


The range range function returns a finite sequence of values, with different methods giving sequences of different data types, bounds, and intervals, depending on the input arguments. Here, range(0.0, 1/α; length = 400) is a method of the range function that returns a sequence of value between \(0.0\) and \(\frac{1}{\alpha}\)
length = 400 represent the the number of samples/points in the function call range(…, length = 400) This forms a “grid” (a collection of regular systematic samples) on the x-axis. The y-values come from passing each y-value to the function to get the result. Instead of a systematic sample, we can randomly sample from the same range.
Instead of a systematic grid with range, generate a collection of \(x\)-coordinates of the same size by sampling independently from a uniform distribution over the same range and type using rand. Calculate the corresponding \(y\)-coordinates in the same way, by using map and the function. Visualize the results using scatter.
Here we both regularly (grid) and randomly sample 10 points from between 0.0 and 1/alpha:
julia> x_vals1 = collect(range(0.0, 1/α, length=10)) 10-element Vector{Float64}: 0.0 0.2222222222222222 0.4444444444444444 0.6666666666666666 0.8888888888888888 1.1111111111111112 1.3333333333333333 1.5555555555555556 1.7777777777777777 2.0
julia> x_vals2 = rand(0.0:0.01:1/α, 10) 10-element Vector{Float64}: 0.55 1.72 1.09 0.38 0.33 0.38 1.42 1.24 0.76 0.98 These all form one set of coordinates. The other, comes from applying the function to these:
y_vals1 = map(x -> ???, x_vals1) y_vals2 = map(x -> ???, x_vals2) Randomly sampling values from the model’s x value range as opposed to a regular grid makes sense when the range is huge (e.g. \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\)), and we cannot possibly cover it all with a grid.



Exercise 3

Simulate 1000 independent rolls of a single fair six-sided die by using rand to sample from an integer value in \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\).

text:
Proficiencies

Sampling a single random value of a specified numeric type (e.g., Int, Float64) using rand.
Sampling multiple random values of the specified type and length using rand.
Sampling uniformly from \((0, 1]\) using rand()
How to sample a vector of independent uniform random Float64 values in \((0, 1]\) by passing a length to rand.
How to sample a matrix of independent uniform random Float64 values in \((0, 1]\) by passing row and column dimensions to rand.
How to sample uniformly at random from a defined integer range using rand with a range argument (e.g., rand(-500:500, n)).
How to sample uniformly at random from an explicit collection of values (e.g., an array of floats or characters) using rand.












TipFunctions vs methods in Julia



In Julia, a function is a operation that can accept inputs and returns outputs. A function of a particular name (e.g. range, rand, my_custom_function) may have a number of different methods, or implementation that are distinguished by the pattern of arguments the function takes (called the signature of the function).
See: Julia: Functions, methods, and signatures

The rand function is the function we will most often use to generate random variates of different shapes, and sizes and characteristics. The rand function has a number of different methods, that is, different approaches for generating random values of various different data types, structures, and ranges, depending on the arguments passed to it.



The core Julia library provides rand methods that generate values by sampling them from ranges and collections under a uniform probability distribution. Packages such as Distributions.jl, covered separately, provide the ability to sample random values from a broader range of distributions.






TipProbability distributions











Sampling a random integer between its smallest and largest representible value with uniform random probability:
rand(Int)

Multidimensional collections of values can be generated by the syntax, rand(Type, n, m), where n is the number of rows and m the number of columns.

We can use methods of the rand function that take range objects to constrain the values to particular ranges. Instead of a type (Int, Float64, and so on), we can pass the rand function a range object to sample with uniform probability from the intervals or collections of values represented by the range object.
Sampling 10 integer values from the closed interval [-5, 5] with uniform random probability:

A uniform distribution between value \(a\) and \(b\), with support of continuous values in the real interval \([a, b]\) is denoted

\]
A uniform distribution between value \(a\) and \(b\), with support of integer values in a finite set of integers in the interval \([a, b]\), is denoted

The hist function provides a variety of methods to visualize data in histogram formats.

y_vals1 = map(x -> ???, x_vals1) y_vals2 = map(x -> ???, x_vals2) Randomly sampling values from the model’s x value range as opposed to a regular grid makes sense when the range is huge (e.g. \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\)), and we cannot possibly cover it all with a grid.

title: Working with randomness and probabilities
section: 2 Simulating a Bernoulli trial with rand
text:
2 Simulating a Bernoulli trial with rand
We can use rand(), which returns a uniformly distributed real value in \([0, 1)\) to determine whether or not an event of given probability occurs or not in a particular sample (outcome, realization, draw, run, etc.) of a random system.
For an event with some given probability value, if the value returned by the rand() function is less than this value we consider the event to have occurred. By default then, if the result of rand() is greater than this value, the event has not occured.





Consider 1000 samples from a uniform distribution on a subset of real number line between \(0\) and \(1\).
If we consider a uniform distribution on a subset of real number line between \(0\) and \(1\), and divide it at \(p\) of various values, we can see the larger segment of the range assigned to one or the other outcome depending the parameter.
If we consider that rand() will return a sample anywhere in that range with equal probability, we can see how a larger \(p\) means a value will fall in the part of the range that maps to the first outcome and vice versa.
if the result of arand() is less than \(p\), then we have simulated a sample in which the event has occurred, and conversely, if greater than or equal to \(p\), to not have occured.
For example, consider the classical Bernoulli trial modeling an idealized fair coin toss, where there are two possible outcomes, “heads” or “tails”, with the probability of “heads” in any single realization being given by the model parameter \(p=0.5\).
The short-hand Julia expression for this is:

rand() < 0.5 ? "heads" : "tails"

"heads"


Or, for a more readable, flexible, extensible, as well as maintanable, we define a named function that takes an argument which allows us to specify the probability parameter:

function bernoulli(p::Float64)::String
    if rand() < p
        "heads"
    else
        "tails"
    end
end
bernoulli(0.5)

"tails"

title: The computing ecosystem
text:
2 File-system essentials

Proficiencies
File system concepts:

Spatial metaphor of “location” in a hierarchical tree of folders and files.
The current working directory.
Specifying a location using a “path” string.
Specifying absolute vs. relative paths.
Program or executable pathss.
Standard file-system organization



Every file you will use in this course — a Julia script, a downloaded dataset, a saved figure — lives somewhere on a computer’s file system. Before writing a line of Julia, it helps to have a precise vocabulary for where things are and how to say so in text. This chapter builds that vocabulary. The next chapter, on the shell, puts it to work.

2.1 Files and directories







Term
Meaning




File
A named unit of stored data: a Julia script, a CSV table, an image, a PDF.


Directory (folder)
A container that groups files and other directories.


Path
A text string that names the location of a file or directory.


Root
The single directory that contains, directly or indirectly, everything else.



“Directory” and “folder” name the same thing. “Directory” is the older, more technical term, used by the shell and by Julia; “folder” is the term most graphical file managers show on screen. This text uses both, and treats them as synonyms.
A file system organizes files by nesting directories inside other directories, to any depth. A directory can hold files, other directories, or both. This nesting is what makes it possible to have a clean_data.jl file in a scripts directory and a completely different clean_data.jl file in a data directory, without either overwriting the other: the 2 files have the same name but different locations.


2.2 The directory tree
Because directories can nest inside directories, the whole arrangement forms a tree. One directory, the root, sits at the top; everything else hangs beneath it, directly or through a chain of intermediate directories.
project/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── observations.csv
│   └── processed/
│       └── observations_clean.csv
├── scripts/
│   ├── clean_data.jl
│   └── analyze.jl
├── figures/
│   └── summary_plot.png
└── Project.toml
Reading this diagram: project is a directory containing 2 other directories (data, scripts) and 1 file (Project.toml). data in turn contains 2 directories, raw and processed, each holding 1 file. Indentation and the tree lines show nesting; they are not part of any name.
A few relational terms are useful:








Term
Meaning
In the example above




Parent directory
The directory that directly contains a given file or directory.
data is the parent of raw.


Subdirectory / child
A directory directly contained by another.
raw and processed are subdirectories of data.


Ancestor
Any directory reached by repeatedly following parents upward.
project is an ancestor of observations.csv.



“Climbing” the tree means moving toward the root, from a file or directory to its parent, grandparent, and so on. “Descending” means moving from a directory into one of its subdirectories.







NoteThe tree has more than 1 root



The diagram above shows a project’s root — the top-level directory of one particular collection of files. The whole file system also has its own single root, discussed later in this chapter under standard file-system organization. A project’s top directory is not the same thing as the file system’s root, even though both are informally called “the root” of whatever tree is under discussion.



2.3 Paths: writing a location as text
A path is a string that specifies the location of a file or directory by naming the sequence of directories that lead to it.
data/raw/observations.csv
This path names 3 things in sequence, separated by a path separator: the directory data, the directory raw inside it, and the file observations.csv inside that. The separator is a forward slash, /, on macOS and Linux, and traditionally a backslash, \, on Windows, although modern Windows tools, including Julia, generally also accept forward slashes.








Component
Example
Role




Separator
/ (macOS, Linux) or \ (Windows)
Marks the boundary between 1 directory name and the next.


Directory name
data, raw
1 segment of the path.


File name
observations.csv
The final segment, naming the file itself.


Extension
.csv
The suffix of the file name, usually indicating file type.










TipJulia hides the separator problem for you



Writing separators by hand is fragile: a path built with / breaks on a system that expects \, and vice versa. Once Julia is in the picture, joinpath builds paths using whatever separator the current operating system expects, so code that constructs paths does not need to hard-code either character. This is covered when program files are introduced.



2.4 Absolute paths and relative paths
A path can be written in 2 ways: starting from the file system’s root, or starting from wherever the reader currently is.








Kind
Starts from
Example




Absolute path
The file-system root
/home/student/project/data/raw/observations.csv


Relative path
The current location
data/raw/observations.csv



An absolute path always identifies the same file or directory, no matter where it is written or read from — it fully specifies the route from the root. A relative path is only meaningful together with a starting point. The same relative path, data/raw/observations.csv, refers to different files depending on where it is interpreted from: from inside project, it reaches project/data/raw/observations.csv; from inside some other directory that happens to also contain a data subdirectory, it reaches a completely different file.
Absolute paths on macOS and Linux begin with /, the root itself:
/home/student/project/data/raw/observations.csv
Absolute paths on Windows begin with a drive letter:
C:\Users\student\project\data\raw\observations.csv
Relative paths never begin with a separator (on macOS or Linux) or a drive letter (on Windows); they begin directly with a name.







Question
Use




Will this path be read from a known, fixed location?
Absolute path


Is this path being written relative to a project folder that might live anywhere?
Relative path


Am I sharing this path with someone using a different computer?
Relative path



Relative paths are usually preferred for scripts and shared projects, since an absolute path baked into a script only works on the one computer where it was written. Absolute paths are useful for referring, unambiguously, to a specific location regardless of context — for example, when telling someone else exactly where a file lives.


2.5 The current working directory
Every running program — a shell session, a Julia session, a script being executed — has, at any moment, a current working directory: the location in the tree that relative paths are interpreted against. This is the “starting point” referred to in the definition of a relative path above.
The current working directory is not a property of a file or a program’s code; it is a property of the running session. The same script, executed twice from 2 different working directories, can resolve the same relative path to 2 different files. This is a common source of “file not found” confusion for beginners, and it is worth internalizing early: when a relative path does not seem to work, the first question is always what is the current working directory right now?
The next chapter shows how to ask the shell this question directly, and later chapters show the equivalent inside Julia. For now, the concept to hold onto is that “current working directory” names a real, specific location, even though it is not written down anywhere in the path string itself — it is implicit context that has to be tracked.


2.6 Special path segments: ., .., and ~
A few short symbols have fixed meanings inside a path, on macOS, Linux, and Windows alike.







Symbol
Meaning




.
The current directory itself.


..
The parent of the current directory.


~
The current user’s home directory (macOS, Linux; not standard on Windows).



These symbols can be combined with ordinary path segments. From inside project/scripts, the file project/data/raw/observations.csv can be reached with:
../data/raw/observations.csv
.. steps up from scripts to project; data/raw/observations.csv then descends back down from there. Repeating ../.. steps up 2 levels, and so on.
~ is a convenient shorthand for “wherever my home directory is,” which differs from user to user and machine to machine:
~/project/data/raw/observations.csv
is equivalent to, for example,
/home/student/project/data/raw/observations.csv
on a machine where the home directory is /home/student.


2.7 Program and executable paths
A program that can be run — julia, python, a compiled application — is, itself, a file: an executable file, sitting at some specific path on the file system, exactly like a data file or a script. Typing a bare name such as julia at a shell prompt does not magically invoke “the Julia program” in the abstract; it asks the shell to locate a file named julia (or julia.exe on Windows) among a specific list of directories it is configured to search, and then run that file.
That list of directories is called the search path, stored in an environment variable conventionally named PATH. When installation instructions say “make sure julia is on your PATH,” they mean: the directory containing the julia executable file must be one of the directories the shell searches when it sees the bare name julia typed as a command.
A program can also be run by giving its full path directly, bypassing the search entirely:
/usr/local/bin/julia
or, on Windows,
C:\Users\student\AppData\Local\Programs\Julia-1.12.6\bin\julia.exe
Both forms run the same executable file. The bare name is shorter and is what people normally type; the full path is unambiguous and does not depend on how the search path happens to be configured. The next chapter shows a shell command that reports exactly which file a bare program name resolves to.


2.8 Standard file-system organization
Every mainstream operating system organizes its file system according to broadly similar conventions, even though the exact names differ.








Concept
macOS / Linux
Windows




File-system root
/
1 root per drive, e.g. C:\


Home directory
/home/username (Linux) or /Users/username (macOS)
C:\Users\username


Home directory shorthand
~
%USERPROFILE% (less commonly typed by hand)


Desktop, Documents, Downloads
Subdirectories of the home directory
Subdirectories of the home directory


Installed applications
/Applications (macOS); scattered under /usr, /opt (Linux)
C:\Program Files



For this course, the directory that matters most is the home directory: it is where a user account’s files live by default, where downloaded installers land (typically inside a Downloads subdirectory), and where per-user configuration for tools such as Julia is stored.







TipHidden files and dotfiles



On macOS and Linux, any file or directory whose name begins with a period, such as .gitignore or .bashrc, is treated as hidden: it is not shown by default in graphical file managers or in a plain directory listing. Hidden files are not special or protected — they are ordinary files that conventionally stay out of the way of everyday browsing, usually because they hold configuration rather than content a user edits directly.
Once Julia is installed, it keeps its packages and per-user configuration in a hidden directory named .julia inside the home directory (~/.julia). This is covered again when packages and environments are introduced.



2.9 Common pitfalls







Symptom
Likely cause




A path that works on one computer fails on another.
An absolute path was used where a relative one was needed.


A file “disappears” after a script runs from a different folder.
The current working directory was not what was assumed.


A path with a space in it fails when typed at a shell prompt.
Unquoted spaces are treated as separating multiple arguments; the next chapter covers quoting.


A file that should be there is not shown in a listing.
The file’s name begins with . and is being hidden by default.


A path that worked on Linux fails, case-related, on another Linux machine.
macOS and Windows file systems are usually case-insensitive by default; Linux file systems are case-sensitive, so Data.csv and data.csv are 2 different files.





2.10 Practice exercises

Exercise 1
Using the tree diagram from this chapter,
project/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── observations.csv
│   └── processed/
│       └── observations_clean.csv
├── scripts/
│   ├── clean_data.jl
│   └── analyze.jl
├── figures/
│   └── summary_plot.png
└── Project.toml
write:

The path to observations.csv, relative to project.
The path to clean_data.jl, relative to data/raw.
The path to summary_plot.png, relative to data/processed.
An absolute path to Project.toml, assuming project is located at /home/student/project.




Exercise 2
Open your operating system’s graphical file manager (Finder on macOS, File Explorer on Windows, or your Linux distribution’s equivalent) and navigate to your home directory.

Write down its absolute path.
Locate your Desktop and Downloads folders and write down their absolute paths.
Identify whether these are written relative to /, ~, or a drive letter such as C:\, and explain why.




Exercise 3
For each pair below, state whether the second path is absolute or relative to the first, and explain how you can tell just from its form, without knowing anything about the file system it describes.

Starting point: /home/student/project. Path: ../shared-data/genomes.fasta
Starting point: C:\Users\student\project. Path: C:\Users\student\archive\genomes.fasta
Starting point: ~/project/scripts. Path: ~/project/data/genomes.fasta





2.11 Further reading

Julia: Filesystem functions
Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (Wikipedia)
Software Carpentry: The Unix Shell — Files and Directories

title: The computing ecosystem
text:
3 Shell essentials

Proficiencies

How to open a “shell” instance (“terminal”, “command-line”).
How to identify the current working directory path.
How to list the contents of the current working directory.
How to list the contents of any directory given relative and absolute paths.
How to change the current working directory based on:

relative paths
absolute paths

How to specify the location of a directory or a file as an argument to a program using both relative paths and absolute paths.
How to communicate or correlate file and directory locations presented in the operating system graphical interface (GUI) as or with path string specifiers in the shell.
How to create a new directory.
How to rename or move a directory.
How to rename or move a file.
How to copy a directory.
How to copy a file.



The previous chapter described paths and locations as text; this chapter puts that vocabulary to work. A shell is a program that reads commands typed as text and executes them, one line at a time. It is the primary tool for moving around the directory tree, inspecting what is there, and rearranging it — and it is also how Julia itself gets started, as the next section of this text will show.







NoteShell, terminal, and command line



These 3 terms are often used interchangeably by beginners, and this text does the same where the distinction does not matter. Precisely: a terminal is the window or application that displays text input and output; a shell is the program running inside it that actually reads and executes commands (common shells include bash, zsh, and PowerShell); “the command line” informally refers to the whole activity of typing commands into a shell.


3.1 Opening a shell








Platform
Program
How to open it




macOS
Terminal
Open from Applications → Utilities, or search “Terminal” in Spotlight.


Linux
Varies by desktop environment — GNOME Terminal, Konsole, xterm, or similar
Search “Terminal” in the application menu, or use the usual keyboard shortcut for your desktop environment.


Windows
Windows Terminal or PowerShell
Search “Terminal” or “PowerShell” in the Start menu.


Any platform
VS Code’s integrated terminal
Menu: View → Terminal, or the backtick shortcut (Ctrl-` / Cmd-`).



Any of these gives access to a shell. This text’s examples work in a Unix-style shell — bash or zsh, the default on macOS and Linux, and also available on Windows through VS Code’s integrated terminal, Git Bash, or Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). A short table of PowerShell and Command Prompt equivalents for Windows users who are not using a Unix-style shell appears near the end of this chapter.


3.2 The shell prompt
Once a shell is open, it displays a prompt and waits for input. A typical prompt looks something like:
student@laptop:~/projects/20260813--screech-owl$
showing the user name, the machine name, the current working directory (~/projects/20260813--screech-owl, using the ~ shorthand from the previous chapter), and a trailing symbol, here $, that marks where typed text will appear. The exact appearance varies by shell, configuration, and operating system.






NotePrompt markers are not part of the command



Because the full prompt is long and varies by machine, this text abbreviates it to a single $ in examples. $ identifies where a line is typed; it is not typed itself.
$ pwd
means: type pwd, then press Enter. Do not type the $.


Type a command and press Enter; the shell runs it, prints any output, and shows a fresh prompt.


3.3 Identifying the current working directory: pwd
The previous chapter introduced the current working directory as a concept: the location that relative paths are resolved against. The shell command pwd (“print working directory”) reports it directly.
$ pwd
/home/student/projects/20260813--screech-owl
This is always an absolute path. Whenever a relative path does not seem to point where expected, running pwd first is the standard way to check the assumption behind it.


3.4 Listing directory contents: ls
ls (“list”) shows the contents of a directory. With no arguments, it lists the current working directory:
$ ls
data  src  figures  Project.toml
Two flags are worth knowing early:







Flag
Effect




ls -l
“Long” listing: 1 entry per line, with type, permissions, size, and modification date.


ls -a
Include hidden entries — files and directories whose names begin with ., as described in the previous chapter.


ls -la
Both combined.



$ ls -l
drwxr-xr-x  4 student student  128 Aug 20 09:14 data
drwxr-xr-x  3 student student   96 Aug 20 09:14 src
drwxr-xr-x  2 student student   64 Aug 20 09:14 figures
-rw-r--r--  1 student student  312 Aug 20 09:15 Project.toml

3.4.1 Listing another directory: relative and absolute arguments
ls accepts a path as an argument, and lists that location instead of the current working directory — using exactly the relative and absolute paths from the previous chapter:
$ ls data
processed  raw

$ ls ./data
processed  raw

$ ls /home/student/projects/20260813--screech-owl/data
processed  raw
All 3 commands above list the same directory, from the same starting working directory: the first 2 use relative paths (data and the equivalent, more explicit ./data), the third uses an absolute path.



3.5 Changing the current working directory: cd
cd (“change directory”) updates the shell’s current working directory.
$ pwd
/home/student/projects/20260813--screech-owl

$ cd data
$ pwd
/home/student/projects/20260813--screech-owl/data
cd accepts the same relative and absolute paths, and the same special segments, as any other path.







Command
Effect




cd data
Descend into the data subdirectory of the current location.


cd ..
Move up to the parent directory.


cd /home/student/projects/20260813--screech-owl
Jump directly to an absolute path.


cd ~ or cd (no argument)
Return to the home directory.


cd -
Return to the previous working directory (bash and zsh).



$ cd data/raw
$ pwd
/home/student/projects/20260813--screech-owl/data/raw

$ cd ../..
$ pwd
/home/student/projects/20260813--screech-owl

$ cd
$ pwd
/home/student

$ cd -
/home/student/projects/20260813--screech-owls
Following cd with pwd (or ls) to confirm the new location is a good habit to confirm your location is correct, avoiding the potential for much frustration (when some commands do not work) or horrific tragedy (when some commands do work, but on the wrong files)


3.6 Invoking a program with a path location as an argument
ls data above is 1 example of a more general pattern: many programs take a path as an argument, telling them where to look. The same relative-versus-absolute choice applies no matter which program is being run. We might have a
$ julia src/analyze.jl
$ julia /home/student/project/crc/analyze.jl
Both invoke the same file, using the same two forms of path already introduced.


3.7 Correlating shell paths with the graphical file manager
The graphical file manager (Finder, File Explorer, or similar) and the shell describe the same file system, but show locations differently: one as icons and a navigable window, the other as text. Being able to translate between them is useful when, for instance, a data file was downloaded through a browser and now needs to be reached from a script.

macOS Finder: enable View → Show Path Bar to see the full path of the current folder at the bottom of the window; clicking the folder’s name in the window’s title bar shows a dropdown of its location in the hierarchy.
Windows File Explorer: click once in the address bar to reveal the full path as editable text, or right-click the address bar for a “Copy address as text” option.
Linux file managers: most (Nautilus, Dolphin, and others) support typing Ctrl-L to reveal or edit the path directly, or a path-bar toggle similar to Finder’s.








TipDrag a folder into the terminal



Most terminal applications, including Terminal on macOS, GNOME Terminal on Linux, and Windows Terminal, insert a file or folder’s path as plain text if its icon is dragged from the file manager into the terminal window. This is a quick way to get an exact absolute path without typing it by hand.



3.8 Creating a new directory: mkdir
$ mkdir results
creates a new, empty directory named results inside the current working directory. Creating a nested directory whose parents do not yet exist requires the -p flag:
$ mkdir -p results/2026-08-25/figures
-p creates every missing directory along the path — here, results, then 2026-08-25 inside it, then figures inside that — in 1 step, and does not raise an error if some of them already exist. Without -p, mkdir refuses to create a directory whose parent does not yet exist.


3.9 Copying files and directories: cp
cp source destination copies a file:
$ cp observations.csv observations_backup.csv
The destination can also be a directory, in which case the file is copied into it, keeping its original name:
$ cp data/raw/observations.csv data/processed/
Copying a directory requires the -r (“recursive”) flag, so that its contents are copied along with it:
$ cp -r data data_backup
Without -r, cp refuses to copy a directory.


3.10 Moving and renaming: mv
Unix-style shells use a single command, mv, for both moving a file to a different location and renaming it in place. This is not 2 unrelated features that happen to share a name: a rename is a move, to a new name within the same directory.
$ mv draft.jl analysis.jl
moves draft.jl to analysis.jl in the same directory — a rename.
$ mv analysis.jl scripts/
moves analysis.jl into the scripts directory, keeping its name — a move.
$ mv data data_archive
renames the whole data directory to data_archive; unlike cp, mv does not need a -r flag to move a directory, since nothing inside it is being duplicated.






Importantcp and mv overwrite silently



If the destination of cp or mv already exists, it is overwritten without confirmation and without a way to recover the original through the shell. Running ls on the destination first, before copying or moving into it, is a cheap habit that avoids this. Deleting files is intentionally not covered in this chapter; it is a more consequential operation than the 4 covered here, and is better introduced together with the safeguards around it.




3.11 Finding a program’s executable path: which
The previous chapter described running a program by its bare name as really asking the shell to search a list of directories, PATH, for a matching executable file. which reports the result of that search directly:
$ which julia
/usr/local/bin/julia
If no matching file is found anywhere on PATH, which reports nothing found, which is the same failure that produces a “command not found” error when the name is actually run.


3.12 Windows equivalents
Readers using PowerShell or Command Prompt directly, rather than a Unix-style shell, can use the following equivalents for the commands introduced above.









Task
bash / zsh
PowerShell
Command Prompt (cmd.exe)




Show working directory
pwd
pwd (alias for Get-Location)
cd (no argument)


List contents
ls
ls (alias for Get-ChildItem)
dir


Change directory
cd
cd
cd


Create directory
mkdir
mkdir
mkdir


Copy a file
cp
Copy-Item
copy


Copy a directory
cp -r
Copy-Item -Recurse
xcopy /E


Move or rename
mv
Move-Item / Rename-Item
move / ren


Find an executable
which
Get-Command
where



PowerShell aliases several Unix-style names (pwd, ls, cp, mv) to its own underlying commands, so the left and middle columns often work identically in practice; cmd.exe does not, and uses its own distinct set of names.


3.13 A recommended beginner workflow

Open a shell.
Run pwd to confirm the starting location.
Run ls to see what is already there.
Use cd to reach the intended project directory.
Use mkdir to create any missing directories before writing files into them.
After any cp or mv, run ls again to confirm the result matches what was intended.



3.14 Common error messages








Symptom
Likely cause
First check




command not found
The program name is misspelled, or its directory is not on PATH.
which the-command-name

The path is wrong, or relative to an unexpected working directory.
pwd, then ls on the intended parent directory.

The current user does not have the needed access rights.
Confirm the location and whether elevated permissions are genuinely required.


Is a directory

Add -r.

Add -p.


mkdir: cannot create directory ... File exists
A directory with that name is already there.
ls to confirm; mkdir -p tolerates this case.

title: Working with data tables
text:
1 What is tabular data?
Datasets are often organized as tables: rectangular grids of values where each row represents one observation (a specimen, a time-point, a site, a sequencing read) and each column represents one variable or attribute measured for every observation (body mass, collection date, latitude, base-call quality score).







TipRows are observations; columns are variables



This convention — one row per observation, one column per variable — is called tidy data. It is the standard expected by virtually every data-analysis and plotting library you will encounter. Keeping your own data in this form from the start will save a great deal of reformatting later.

A small example of a tabular dataset:



specimen_id
species
body_mass_g
collection_year




BM_001
Peromyscus maniculatus
21.4
2019


BM_002
Peromyscus leucopus
23.1
2019


BM_003
Mus musculus
18.7
2020



Three rows, four columns. Each row is one specimen; each column is one thing we recorded about every specimen.

title: Working with data tables
text:
2 File formats for tabular data






NoteSample files in different formats




Comma-separated value (“CSV”) files, with extension .csv: specimens_10.csv
Tab-separated values (“TSV”) files, with extension .tsv: specimens_10.tsv
Excel files: specimens_10.xlsx



Tabular datasets are stored in a variety of file formats. The format you receive will determine which Julia function you use to load it, so it is worth being able to identify them.

2.1 CSV and its variants
The most common plain-text format for tabular data is CSV (comma-separated values). A CSV file stores the table as lines of text. The first line is typically a header listing the column names; every subsequent line is one row of data. Values within each line are separated by a delimiter — most often a comma (,), giving the format its name, though tabs (\t) and semicolons (;) are also common.







NoteInspecting a CSV file directly



Because CSV files are plain text, you can read them in any text editor or print their first few lines in the shell:
head -5 specimens.csv
or in Julia:
open("specimens.csv") do f
    for _ in 1:5
        println(readline(f))
    end
end
This is useful for confirming the delimiter, checking whether there is a header row, and spotting any obvious formatting issues before you try to parse the file.

A CSV file corresponding to the table above would look like this:
specimen_id,species,body_mass_g,collection_year
BM_001,Peromyscus maniculatus,21.4,2019
BM_002,Peromyscus leucopus,23.1,2019
BM_003,Mus musculus,18.7,2020
A TSV (tab-separated values) file is identical in structure, but with tab characters between values rather than commas:
specimen_id⟶species⟶body_mass_g⟶collection_year
BM_001⟶Peromyscus maniculatus⟶21.4⟶2019
Both extensions — .csv and .tsv — are strong signals of the format, but always confirm by opening the file.


2.2 Excel files
Excel workbooks (.xlsx, and the older .xls) store tables in a binary format: you cannot read them as plain text. They can contain multiple worksheets in a single file. When working with Excel data in Julia, you will need to specify both the file path and which worksheet you want.

title: Working with data tables
section: 3 Setting up your Julia environment for tabular data
text:
3 Setting up your Julia environment for tabular data
Before we can work with tabular data, we need to install the DataFrames.jl, which gives us the DataFrame object type, In addition, we will install CSV.jl and XLSX.jl to allow us to access data stored in some common file formats. Installation is done through Julia’s built-in package manager, Pkg.
Installations can be done either globally, across your entire Julia ecosystem, or restricted to specific project environments.

3.1 Install globally
A global install makes the package available in any Julia session on your machine, regardless of which directory you are in or which project environment you have activated.
using Pkg
Pkg.add(["DataFrames", "CSV", "XLSX"])
You only need to do this once per Julia version. After installation, using DataFrames will work in any session.


3.2 Install for a project
If you are working inside a project directory — one that contains a Project.toml file — activate the project environment first, then add the packages. This records the dependency in Project.toml and pins exact versions in Manifest.toml, so anyone who clones the project gets the same package versions you used.
using Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")
Pkg.add(["DataFrames", "CSV", "XLSX"])
Once the environment is active, all subsequent Pkg operations in that session apply to the project rather than to the global environment.

title: Working with data tables
text:
4 The DataFrame type
In Julia, the standard representation of a data table is a DataFrame object from the DataFrames package.
A DataFrame holds a collection of named columns, where each column is a typed Vector. This means every value in a given column must be of the same type (all integers, all floating-point numbers, all strings, and so on), but different columns can have different types — exactly as in a real dataset.
using DataFrames

4.1 Creating a DataFrame manually from column vectors
The most direct way to construct a DataFrame is to pass named column vectors to the DataFrame constructor:

using DataFrames

specimens = DataFrame(
    specimen_id      = ["BM_001", "BM_002", "BM_003"],
    species          = ["Peromyscus maniculatus", "Peromyscus leucopus", "Mus musculus"],
    body_mass_g      = [21.4, 23.1, 18.7],
    collection_year  = [2019, 2019, 2020]
)

Each keyword argument becomes a column: the argument name is the column name, and the vector on the right is the column’s data. All vectors must have the same length.







TipColumn types are inferred automatically



Julia infers the element type of each column from the vector you supply. ["BM_001", "BM_002", "BM_003"] becomes a Vector{String} column; [21.4, 23.1, 18.7] becomes a Vector{Float64} column. You can confirm the types of all columns at once with describe(df), discussed below.

title: Working with data tables
text:
5 Reading tabular data from files
In practice you will almost never type your data in by hand. Most of the time you will load it from a file written by an instrument, a database export, a collaborator’s spreadsheet, or a public data repository.

5.1 Reading CSV files with CSV.jl
The CSV package provides the CSV.read function, which parses a delimited text file and, when combined with DataFrame, returns the result as a DataFrame:
using CSV, DataFrames

specimens = CSV.read("specimens.csv", DataFrame)
CSV.read takes two required arguments: the path to the file, and the sink type that determines what kind of object the parsed data is placed into. Passing DataFrame as the sink is by far the most common usage.







NoteCommon keyword arguments for CSV.read



CSV.read accepts a large number of optional keyword arguments for handling real-world files that do not follow a perfectly clean format:
# File uses semicolons as the delimiter
CSV.read("data.csv", DataFrame; delim = ';')

# File uses tabs as the delimiter
CSV.read("data.tsv", DataFrame; delim = '\t')

# Skip the first two lines (e.g., a metadata header)
CSV.read("data.csv", DataFrame; skipto = 3)

# Treat "NA" and "" as missing values
CSV.read("data.csv", DataFrame; missingstring = ["NA", ""])

# File has no header row; supply column names manually
CSV.read("data.csv", DataFrame; header = ["id", "mass", "year"])
When a file refuses to parse cleanly, these keyword arguments are the first place to look.

For a TSV file, specify the delimiter explicitly:
specimens = CSV.read("specimens.tsv", DataFrame; delim = '\t')


5.2 Reading Excel files with XLSX.jl
The XLSX package provides access to Excel workbooks. The XLSX.readtable function reads one worksheet and returns it in a form that can be passed directly to the DataFrame constructor:
using XLSX, DataFrames

specimens = DataFrame(XLSX.readtable("specimens.xlsx", "Sheet1"))
The second argument to XLSX.readtable is the name of the worksheet to read.







TipListing the worksheets in a workbook



If you do not know the names of the worksheets in an Excel file, you can inspect them:
xf = XLSX.readxlsx("specimens.xlsx")
XLSX.sheetnames(xf)
This returns a Vector{String} listing the names of all worksheets in the workbook.

title: Working with data tables
text:
7 Selecting columns
Once you have a DataFrame in memory, the most fundamental operation is selecting the columns you want to work with.

7.1 Selecting a single column as a Vector
Use the . accessor or square-bracket syntax with a Symbol or String:

specimens.body_mass_g          # returns a Vector{Float64}

3-element Vector{Float64}:
 21.4
 23.1
 18.7



specimens[!, :body_mass_g]     # identical result

3-element Vector{Float64}:
 21.4
 23.1
 18.7



specimens[!, "body_mass_g"]    # also identical

3-element Vector{Float64}:
 21.4
 23.1
 18.7









Tip! vs : as the row selector



In DataFrames indexing, the first argument selects rows and the second selects columns. Using ! as the row selector means all rows, without copying — you get a direct reference to the underlying column vector. Using : also selects all rows, but returns a copy. For read-only inspection, ! is fine and slightly more efficient. When you intend to modify the values in the returned vector and do not want to affect the original DataFrame, use :.



7.2 Selecting multiple columns as a new DataFrame
Pass a Vector of column names to get a new DataFrame containing only those columns:

8 Filtering rows
To extract the subset of rows that satisfy some condition, use boolean indexing.

8.1 Boolean indexing
Constructing a logical (boolean) condition over a column produces a Vector{Bool} — a vector of true/false values, one per row:

specimens.collection_year .== 2019

3-element BitVector:
 1
 1
 0


Passing this boolean vector as the row index returns only the rows where the condition is true:

specimens[specimens.collection_year .== 2019, :]

NoteBroadcasting with .



The . before comparison operators (.==, .>, .<=, and so on) is Julia’s broadcasting syntax. It applies the operator element-wise across the entire vector, rather than trying to compare the whole vector to a scalar at once. You will need this . prefix whenever applying a scalar comparison across a column.
# ✓ correct: element-wise comparison
specimens.body_mass_g .> 20.0

# ✗ will error: comparing a Vector to a scalar without broadcasting
specimens.body_mass_g > 20.0

Combining multiple conditions uses & (and) and | (or), with each condition wrapped in parentheses:

specimens[(specimens.body_mass_g .> 20.0) .& (specimens.collection_year .== 2019), :]

Assignment with df.new_column = ... modifies the DataFrame in place, changing the original object. Many DataFrames functions — select, filter, transform — return a new DataFrame instead of modifying the original. This is the standard functional style and is generally preferred because it makes it easy to trace where each transformation happened. Use in-place assignment sparingly and deliberately.



9.2 Adding a column derived from existing columns using transform
The transform function is the idiomatic way to derive new columns from existing ones without modifying the original:

Proficiencies

Using the Julia REPL help mode.
Accessing documentation with @doc.
Searching Julia docstrings.
Reading function signatures and method lists.
Inspecting the types involved in a function call.
Finding version-matched Julia and package documentation.
Preparing a reproducible request for help.
Julia provides documentation through the REPL. This documentation covers functions, types, macros, operators, and language keywords.

title: Julia help and documentation
text:
1 Help mode
Prefix a name with ? to display its documentation directly. For example, the documentation for iseven begins with:
julia> ?iseven
search: iseven isopen isnan isone seek setenv isletter

  iseven(x::Number) -> Bool

  Return true if x is an even integer (that is, an integer divisible by 2),
  and false otherwise.
The docstring also contains calls that can be run directly.
julia> iseven(9)
false

julia> iseven(10)
true
Typing ? by itself changes the prompt to help?> before the name is entered.
julia> ?
help?> iseven
Both forms query the same docstring. Press Backspace at an empty help?> prompt to leave help mode without running a query.
The prompt markers identify where to type each expression. Do not type the prompt markers themselves.

1.1 Querying Julia objects
Help mode accepts several kinds of Julia objects.
help?> Float64

help?> @time

help?> +

help?> begin
Use a qualified name to specify the module that defines an object.
help?> Base.Math.sin
Import a package before querying its documentation.
julia> import DataFrames

julia> ?
help?> DataFrames.DataFrame


1.2 The @doc macro
The @doc macro retrieves documentation from Julia mode. For example, the output from @doc range begins with:
julia> @doc range
  range(start, stop, length)
  range(start, stop; length, step)
  range(start; length, stop, step)
  range(; start, length, stop, step)

  Construct a specialized array with evenly spaced elements and optimized
  storage (an AbstractRange) from the arguments.
At the REPL, @doc range and ?range display the same documentation. @doc can also be used in Julia source code.


1.3 Searching docstrings
Enter a quoted string when the relevant Julia name is unknown.
help?> "matrix multiplication"
A regular expression can search for several related terms.
help?> r"eigen(value|vector)"
These searches use the docstrings loaded in the current session. Import the relevant package before searching its documentation.

title: Julia help and documentation
Julia help and documentation
text:
3 Reading function documentation
Function documentation normally begins with one or more signatures. The range documentation shown above lists several ways to supply start, stop, length, and step.
In the following call, 1 and 10 are positional arguments and length is a keyword argument.
julia> range(1, 10; length=4)
1.0:3.0:10.0

julia> collect(range(1, 10; length=4))
4-element Vector{Float64}:
  1.0
  4.0
  7.0
 10.0
The semicolon separates positional arguments from keyword arguments. An entry such as step=1 in a signature gives the keyword’s default value. Square brackets in a documented signature indicate an optional argument; the brackets are not part of the Julia call.

3.1 Functions and methods
A Julia function can have several methods. Each method accepts a particular combination of positional argument types.
List all methods for a function with methods.
julia> methods(sqrt)
Restrict the result to a tuple of argument types when necessary.
julia> methods(sqrt, (Float64,))
# 1 method for generic function "sqrt" from Base:
 [1] sqrt(x::Union{Float32, Float64})
     @ math.jl:626
Use @which to show the method selected for a particular call.
julia> using InteractiveUtils: @which

julia> @which sqrt(16.0)
sqrt(x::Union{Float32, Float64})
     @ Base.Math math.jl:626
Method lists and source locations can change between Julia versions.

title: Julia help and documentation
text:
4 Inspecting arguments
Method selection depends on argument types. Inspect the values used in the failing or unfamiliar call.
julia> values = [1.0, 4.0, 9.0]

julia> typeof(values)
Vector{Float64}

julia> eltype(values)
Float64

julia> size(values)
(3,)
Common inspection functions include:

typeof(x) for the concrete type of x;
eltype(x) for the element type of a collection;
size(x) for its dimensions;
axes(x) for its valid indices; and
propertynames(x) for its public properties.

For example, sqrt("16") produces a MethodError because no sqrt method accepts a String.
julia> typeof("16")
String

julia> applicable(sqrt, "16")
false
If the string represents a number, parse it before calling sqrt.
julia> sqrt(parse(Float64, "16"))
4.0

title: Julia help and documentation
text:
5 Package documentation and versions
Help mode shows the docstring installed with the current package version. A package manual usually provides longer explanations and complete examples.
Check the active Julia version with:
julia> VERSION
Check the active project and package versions with:
julia> Base.active_project()

julia> import Pkg

julia> Pkg.status()
When consulting online documentation, select the version that matches the current environment.
