title: Geospatial coordinate reference systems
text:
2 Plotting geospatial data with GeoAxis

Proficiencies

Create a GeoMakie geographical figure with given vector data.









TipRecipes





Geospatial data visualization recipes



Geospatial data coordinates are encoded using a coordinate reference systems, and we need to use a special type of plotting axis, the GeoMake.GeoAxis, to convert these values to Cartesian plotting coordinates.







TipCoordinate projections



We say we are projecting the coordinates when we do this, and set of coordinates are said to be in one projection or another, depending on their particular coordinate reference systems.

The GeoMakie.jl.GeoAxis plotting axis automatically manages geospatial coordinate data projection into Cartesian coordinates. It is used with plotting functions instead of the default Cartesian coordinate system Axis when the coordinates in the data need to be projected under a particular geographic coordinate reference system or another for correct visualization or analysis.


using GeoMakie, CairoMakie
1coasts = GeoMakie.coastlines()
2fig = Figure()
3ax = GeoAxis(fig[1,1])
4lines!(ax, coasts)
5# save("coastlines.pdf", fig)
6# save("coastlines.png", fig)
7fig


1

Load coastline data into variable coasts.

2

Create a Figure object: a container for the plots.

3

Create a GeoAxis object: a geospatial CRS-equipped coordinate plotting axis.

4

Plot predefined line data on the given plotting axis.

5

Save to PDF file.

title: Geospatial coordinate reference systems
text:
3 Specifying source and destination projections

Proficiencies

Create a GeoMakie geographical figure with a background of supplied coastline data.
Using PROJ-strings to specify source and destination projections of the data.



The GeoMakie.GeoAxis function that creates and returns a GeoAxis plotting axis allows us to specify both the source data as well the destination coordinate reference systems, along with additional modifiers, using the keyword arguments source and dest, respectively. This allow us to not just to view data in its correct coordinate reference framework, but also transform or reproject the data into arbitrary projections or views. The coordinate reference systems are specified passing special String values called proj-strings (short for “project strings”). By default, GeoMakie.GeoAxis assumes that the source data are longitude and latitude decimal degrees in reference to the WGS84 datum (representation of the Earth’s shape). This corresponds to setting the source proj-string to “+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84”. By default, GeoMakie.GeoAxis also assumes that we want use the Mercator projection under the same datum. This, in turn, corresponds to setting the dest proj-string to “+proj=merc +datum=-WGS84”. As such, the default GeoAxis created without source or dest keyword arguments corresponds to:
using GeoMakie, CairoMakie
fig = Figure()                      
ax = GeoAxis(
  fig[1, 1],
  source = "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84",
  dest   = "+proj=merc +datum=WGS84"
)
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines())   
fig

title: Geospatial coordinate reference systems
text:
4 Plotting alternate projections or views

Proficiencies

Specify alternative map projections using the dest keyword argument of GeoAxis.
Recognize common projection families and their trade-offs (equal-area, conformal, compromise).



The dest proj-string controls the map projection: the mathematical transformation used to flatten the curved surface of the Earth onto a two-dimensional plane. Every projection makes trade-offs, preserving some spatial properties (area, shape, distance, direction) at the cost of others. The proj-string +proj=<name> selects a named projection; additional parameters refine it.

4.1 Equirectangular (Plate Carrée) projection
The equirectangular projection maps longitude directly to the x-axis and latitude directly to the y-axis, producing the familiar rectangular grid of the standard wall map. It is the simplest possible projection and serves as a useful baseline. However, it is neither equal-area not conformal, and distortion increases severely toward the poles.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=longlat")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






4.2 Equal Earth projection
The Equal Earth projection is an equal-area pseudocylindrical projection designed to give continents their correct relative sizes while remaining visually appealing.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






4.3 Robinson projection
The Robinson projection is a compromise projection — it does not perfectly preserve area, shape, or distance, but minimizes overall distortion, giving a visually balanced view of the world. It was used by National Geographic for several decades.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=robin")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






4.4 Mollweide projection
The Mollweide projection is an equal-area elliptical projection. Meridians are elliptical arcs and parallels are horizontal straight lines, with spacing increasing toward the equator to preserve area.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=moll")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






4.5 Orthographic projection
The orthographic projection renders the Earth as it would appear from a distant point in space — a perspective view of a hemisphere. It is neither equal-area nor conformal, but is immediately intuitive.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=ortho +lat_0=20 +lon_0=15")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig




The +lat_0 and +lon_0 parameters set the latitude and longitude of the center of the visible hemisphere. Regions beyond the horizon are automatically excluded from the plot.






TipChoosing a projection








Projection
Proj-string
Preserves
Common use




Mercator
+proj=merc
Shape (conformal)
Navigation, web maps


Equal Earth
+proj=eqearth
Area
Thematic maps


Robinson
+proj=robin
Compromise
General reference


Mollweide
+proj=moll
Area
Scientific/global data


Orthographic
+proj=ortho
—
Perspective/visual


Lambert Azimuthal
+proj=laea
Area
Polar/regional



No projection preserves all properties simultaneously. For biological data — species ranges, diversity gradients, paleoclimate surfaces — equal-area projections are generally preferred because they ensure that regions of equal true area appear as equal area on the map.

title: Geospatial coordinate reference systems
text:
5 Plotting alternate centers or framing

Proficiencies

Re-center a map projection on an arbitrary longitude using the +lon_0 proj-string parameter.
Recognize when re-centering is appropriate for visualizing data in a particular ocean basin or hemisphere.



Every projection has a natural central meridian, the longitude that runs vertically through the center of the map. By default this is \(0°\) (the prime meridian), which places the Pacific Ocean split between the left and right edges of the map. The +lon_0 parameter shifts the central meridian to any target longitude, rotating the entire map so that longitude appears in the center. This is useful when your data are concentrated in a region that would otherwise be split across the map edges — Pacific-basin biodiversity studies, for instance, benefit from centering near \(180°\) or \(-150°\).

5.1 Default centering: \(0°\), the prime meridian

fig = Figure()
1ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=0")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig


1

+lon_0=0 centers the projection on the prime meridian; this is the default and can be omitted.









5.2 Center on \(-100°\) (central North America)

fig = Figure()
1ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=-100")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig


1

+lon_0=-100 centers the map on \(100°\,\text{W}\), roughly the center of North America. The Pacific and Atlantic Oceans are now split at the edges.









5.3 Center on \(120°\) (eastern Asia / western Pacific)

fig = Figure()
1ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=120")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig


1

+lon_0=120 centers the map on \(120°\,\text{E}\), suitable for visualizing data across eastern Asia and the western Pacific.









5.4 Plotting across the antimeridian
Centering the map on \(180°\) (the antimeridian) or plotting data that spans it can produce rendering artifacts: line segments whose endpoints straddle the \(\pm180°\) boundary are drawn as long near-horizontal lines traversing the full width of the plot, because the renderer naively connects the two endpoints without wrapping.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=180")
1lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines())
fig


1

Passing plain GeoMakie.coastlines() without the axis argument does not clip or re-segment coastlines to the current projection, so segments that cross the antimeridian produce long horizontal streaks.









Figure 1




Passing the GeoAxis object into GeoMakie.coastlines(ax) allows GeoMakie to perform axis-aware clipping and re-segmentation of the coastline geometries, resolving most antimeridian artifacts:

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=180")
1lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig


1

Supplying the GeoAxis to coastlines enables axis-aware geometry handling; GeoMakie clips and re-segments features at the projection boundary before rendering, eliminating the crossing artifacts.









Figure 2










TipAntimeridian issues with your own data





The axis-aware GeoMakie.coastlines(ax) approach works for the built-in coastlines dataset. If you are plotting your own polygon or linestring geometries from, say, a GeoDataFrame or a NaturalEarth dataset loaded with NaturalEarth.jl, you will need to handle antimeridian splitting yourself before passing coordinates to lines! or poly!. One approach is to preprocess geometries using GeoInterface.jl-compatible tools to split any segment that crosses \(\pm180°\) into two segments terminating at the boundary:
Plotting across the antimeridian

title: Geospatial coordinate reference systems
text:
6 Regional views with plot limits

Proficiencies

Use the limits keyword argument on GeoAxis to restrict the rendered region to a geographic bounding box.
Identify appropriate longitude and latitude bounds for a region of interest.



The limits keyword argument on GeoAxis accepts a four-element tuple (lon_min, lon_max, lat_min, lat_max) and clips the view to that bounding box.

6.1 Southeast Asia
Southeast Asia spans roughly 92°E to 141°E and 11°S to 28°N.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1];
    limits = (92, 141, -11, 28))
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig




We can use dest = "+proj=longlat" to specify an equirectangular projection.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1];
    dest   = "+proj=longlat",
    limits = (92, 141, -11, 28))
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






6.2 The Americas

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(
    fig[1, 1];
    limits = (-170, -30, -60, 75),
)
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig




We can use the dest keyword to specify a transformation the projection.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(
    fig[1, 1];
    dest = "+proj=longlat",
    limits = (-170, -30, -60, 75),
)
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig






6.3 Australia
Australia spans roughly 112°E to 155°E and 45°S to 10°S.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1];
    limits = (112, 155, -45, -10))
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig




Or, using dest = "+proj=longlat" to specify an equirectangular projection.

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1];
    dest   = "+proj=longlat",
    limits = (112, 155, -45, -10))
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
fig

title: Working with paleobiological fossil distribution data
text:
1 Walkthrough of an example analysis
We will use Julia to visualize the distribution of fossil specimens of particular species or groups of species across space and time. We will focus on the Canidae (the dog family) during the Miocene (about 23 to 5 million years ago), a critical time for mammalian diversification.

Proficiencies

Install Julia packages.
Load Julia packages.
Download fossil occurrence data from the Paleobiology Database.
Clean and curate data to to required standards.
Visualize data




1.1 Install packages
You will only need to do this once for each project environment (including your global project environment which is what you typically would start by default when you execute the julia command).
using Pkg
Pkg.add([ "PaleobiologyDB", "DataFrames", "GeoMakie", "CairoMakie"])


1.2 Load packages

using PaleobiologyDB
using DataFrames
using GeoMakie, CairoMakie



1.3 Download data
We will ask the database for every recorded occurrence of a Canidae fossil from the Miocene epoch.

canids = pbdb_occurrences(
    base_name = "Canidae",
    interval  = "Miocene",
    show      = "full",
    vocab     = "pbdb"
)

println("Found ", nrow(canids), " Miocene canid fossils!")

Found 1347 Miocene canid fossils!



The base_name keyword argument of Canidae filters for occurrences of fossils identified as Canidae and lower taxonomic levels (that is, occurrences of all fossils identified to the level of species or genera as belonging to the Canidae, as well as fossils identified only to the level of family as “Canidae” itself).
The interval keyword argument of Miocene filters for fossil occurrences in the Miocene Epoch.
The show keyword argument of full to specify we want extended information.
The vocab keyword argument of pbdb returns human-readable column names such rather than the raw API codes.



1.4 2: Prepare the data
Real-world data is often messy. Some fossil records may be missing exact GPS coordinates. Before we can make a map, we must remove any rows that lack a latitude or longitude value.

clean_canids = dropmissing(canids, [:lat, :lng])

println("Records with valid coordinates: ", nrow(clean_canids))
println("Records dropped: ", nrow(canids) - nrow(clean_canids))

Records with valid coordinates: 1347
Records dropped: 0




1.5 3: Visualize the data
Now we will plot these points on a world map. In the Miocene the continents were roughly where they are today, but the climate and faunal dispersal corridors were quite different.

fig = Figure()
ax  = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; title = "Miocene Canidae Occurrences")

lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines())  # land reference — without this the plot is blank
scatter!(ax, clean_canids.lng, clean_canids.lat;
         color = :red, markersize = 5)

display(fig)




CairoMakie.Screen{IMAGE}

title: Working with paleobiological fossil distribution data
text:
2 Data acquisition and curation

2.1 The Paleobiology Database
The Paleobiology Database (PBDB) is a community-curated, openly accessible repository of fossil occurrence records spanning the history of life on Earth. Each record — an occurrence — documents that a particular taxon was found at a particular place, in a stratigraphic unit of known geological age. The PBDB currently holds several million such records contributed by researchers worldwide.







TipOccurrences, collections, and taxa



The PBDB organizes its data around three main entities.
A collection is a set of fossils from the same physical locality and stratigraphic context — essentially one fossil site. An occurrence links a taxon to a collection: it records that taxon X was identified in collection Y. A taxon record holds the name, classification, and synonymy information for a biological group.
When we ask for “occurrences of Canidae,” we are asking for every row in the database that links a canid identification to a dated collection, along with the geographic and stratigraphic context of that collection.

The PaleobiologyDB.jl package provides a Julia interface to the PBDB’s web API. Every API endpoint corresponds to a Julia function; calling the function returns a DataFrame.


2.2 Setting up the environment
We will use four packages in this chapter. PaleobiologyDB fetches data from the PBDB API. DataFrames is the standard Julia tabular-data package we used in the previous chapter. CairoMakie is the rendering backend for Makie plots. GeoMakie extends Makie with geographic axes and projections — we introduce it below.
using Pkg
Pkg.add(["PaleobiologyDB", "GeoMakie", "CairoMakie", "DataFrames"])
You can confirm which versions are active at any time:

using Pkg
Pkg.status()

2.3 Exploring the package
Before retrieving any data, it is worth understanding what functions PaleobiologyDB exposes. The package models the PBDB API closely, so listing its exported names gives you a map of the available endpoints:

foreach(println, names(PaleobiologyDB))

pbdb_occurrences is the function we want. Read its documentation directly in the notebook:

@doc pbdb_occurrences

pbdb_occurrences(; kwargs...)
Get information about fossil occurrence records stored in the Paleobiology Database.
Arguments

kwargs...: Filtering and output parameters. Common options include:

limit: Maximum number of records to return (Int or "all").

taxon_name: Return only records with the specified taxonomic name(s).

base_name: Return records for the specified name(s) and all descendant taxa.

lngmin, lngmax, latmin, latmax: Geographic bounding box.

min_ma, max_ma: Minimum and maximum age in millions of years.

interval: Named geologic interval (e.g. "Miocene").

cc: Country/continent codes (ISO two-letter or three-letter).

show: Extra information blocks ("coords", "classext", "ident", etc.). show = "full" for everything.

extids: Set extids = true to show the newer string identifiers.

vocab: Vocabulary for field names ("pbdb" for full names, "com" for short codes).




Returns
A DataFrame with fossil occurrence records matching the query.
Examples

# `taxon_name` retrieves *only* units of this rank
occs = pbdb_occurrences(
    taxon_name="Canis",
    show="full", # all columns
    limit=100,
)

# `base_name` retrieves units of this and nested rank
occs = pbdb_occurrences(
    base_name="Canis",

TipPBDB data service API help



The PaleobiologyDB package includes a built-in help system that mirrors the upstream API documentation, going well beyond what fits in a single function docstring:
using PaleobiologyDB.ApiHelp
names(ApiHelp)
There is even help on using the help system itself:
?ApiHelp
?pbdb_help()
?pbdb_endpoints()
?pbdb_parameters()
?pbdb_fields()
?pbdb_search()
This is particularly useful when you want to know which show blocks are available, what each field name means, or how to construct a bounding-box query.



2.4 Acquiring occurrence data
The primary function for retrieving occurrence records is pbdb_occurrences. Its arguments map directly onto the PBDB API’s query parameters.
When first exploring a new group, request a limited sample so the API call is fast and the result is manageable:

occs = pbdb_occurrences(
    ;   # the ';' indicates end of positional arguments
    base_name = "Carnivora",
    show      = "full",
    vocab     = "pbdb",
    extids    = true,
    limit     = 1000,
)

TipWhat the key arguments do



base_name = "Carnivora" retrieves occurrences for Carnivora and all of its nested descendant taxa. Using taxon_name instead would restrict results to records identified to exactly that name.
show = "full" requests the complete set of response fields, including geographic coordinates, paleocoordinates, classification hierarchy, and stratigraphic details. You can also pass a list of specific blocks — for example show = ["coords", "class"] — to request only what you need.
vocab = "pbdb" uses the long, human-readable field names (e.g. accepted_name, early_interval) rather than the compact API codes.
extids = true returns modern string-style record identifiers (e.g. "occ:12345") rather than bare integers.
limit = 1000 caps the number of records returned. Remove the limit (or set limit = "all") only when you are ready to work with the full dataset.

2.5 Inspecting the data
Before doing anything else, examine what came back.

2.5.1 List the columns of the dataset
The function foreach applies the first argument, a function, to every element of the second argument. Here the first argument is println and the second argument is names(occs). The function call names(occs) returns all the column names of the DataFrame object passed to it, occs. Put altogether: the names(occs) call returns an array of column names, and the foreach function then applies the println function to each element of this array, which prints the column name out to the standard output. The end result is each column name in the occs DataFrame being printed on its own line.

2.6 Data quality assessment
Auditing the data means more than confirming that records are present — it means ensuring the data that is present meets our standards. For paleobiological occurrence data, quality has three distinct dimensions:

Taxonomic resolution — Is the occurrence identified to the rank we need?
Chronological precision — Does the record carry usable age information?
Spatial completeness — Are coordinates available?

We address each in turn.

2.6.1 Taxonomic resolution
Many PBDB occurrences are identified only to genus, family, or higher. For analyses that require species-level identities, those records add noise rather than signal. We define a filter that accepts occurrences at species and subspecies rank:

clean_taxonomy_flt = row -> row.accepted_rank == "species" || row.accepted_rank == "subspecies"

TipEquivalent filtering approaches



DataFrames provides several syntactically different but logically equivalent ways to select rows. The following all produce the same result:
## Boolean indexing
occs_species = occs[occs.accepted_rank .== "species", :]

## filter with a row-function
occs_species = filter(r -> r.accepted_rank == "species", occs)

## subset with a column-function
occs_species = subset(occs, :accepted_rank => ByRow(r -> r == "species"))

## subset with operator shorthand
occs_species = subset(occs, :accepted_rank => ByRow(== "species"))
filter receives the entire row as a NamedTuple, making it natural when the condition involves multiple columns. subset receives one column at a time, which is more composable when building up complex multi-column filters incrementally.



2.6.2 Chronological precision
All PBDB columns that encode dates contain _ma in their names (for millions of years). Selecting them by regex gives a quick overview:

occs_species[:, r".*_ma.*"]

There are several trade-offs when choosing which age columns to require:

direct_ma_value is populated when a collection has been directly dated (e.g. by radiometric methods) — highest precision, lowest coverage.
max_ma / min_ma bracket the age of the stratigraphic unit in which the fossil was found — broader coverage, lower precision.
ma_error captures measurement uncertainty — rarely populated.

Check the data coverage for each:

println("Direct MA measurements: ", nrow(dropmissing(occs_species, r".*direct_ma.*")))
println("Max MA measurements:    ", nrow(dropmissing(occs_species, r".*max_ma.*")))
println("Min MA measurements:    ", nrow(dropmissing(occs_species, r".*min_ma.*")))
println("MA error measurements:  ", nrow(dropmissing(occs_species, r".*ma_error*")))

Direct MA measurements: 11
Max MA measurements:    0
Min MA measurements:    12
MA error measurements:  0


Requiring direct_ma_value maximizes precision but discards the majority of records. For exploratory work, min_ma and max_ma together are the practical choice — they are present for nearly every record that has been properly entered. We retain direct_ma_value as well, since it is useful when available:

occs_with_ages = dropmissing(occs_species, [:direct_ma_value, :max_ma, :min_ma])

The PBDB provides two sets of coordinates for each collection: modern geographic coordinates and reconstructed paleocoordinates (the location of the fossil site at the time of deposition, accounting for plate movement). Check the coverage of each:

modern_coords = nrow(dropmissing(occs_with_ages, [:lng, :lat]))
println("Records with modern coordinates:    ", modern_coords)

paleo_coords = nrow(dropmissing(occs_with_ages, [:paleolng, :paleolat]))
println("Records with paleo-coordinates:     ", paleo_coords)

complete_spatial = nrow(dropmissing(occs_with_ages, [:lng, :lat, :paleolng, :paleolat]))
println("Records with complete spatial data: ", complete_spatial)

Records with modern coordinates:    11
Records with paleo-coordinates:     11
Records with complete spatial data: 11


For visualization on a present-day map, modern coordinates are sufficient. For paleogeographic analyses, paleocoordinates are essential. We require both:

2.7 Missing values in Julia







TipThe Missing type



Julia represents absent data with the singleton value missing, which belongs to the type Missing. A column that might contain absent data has an element type like Union{Missing, Float64} — it can hold either a real number or the missing sentinel.
Arithmetic and comparisons that involve missing propagate it silently:
missing + 1.0    # → missing
missing > 0.0    # → missing
This is intentional: the result of an operation on unknown data is itself unknown. The implication for filtering is that df[df.lng .> -180, :] will silently drop rows where lng is missing, because the comparison returns missing rather than true. Using dropmissing (above) is the explicit, correct approach.

The dropmissing function accepts an optional column list that restricts the check to only those columns — rows with missing in other columns are kept. This deliberate targeting is important: requiring every column to be non-missing is almost always too aggressive. In our quality assessment above, we applied it three times, each time targeting only the columns relevant to that dimension of quality.
Called with no column argument, dropmissing(df) removes any row with a missing value in any column. Use this form only when you genuinely need a fully complete dataset.
Let us confirm that our final filtered dataset is free of missing values in the columns we care about:

describe(occs_clean[:, [:lng, :lat, :paleolng, :paleolat, :min_ma, :max_ma]])

title: Working with paleobiological fossil distribution data
section: 3 Visualization of occurrences in space and time
text:
3 Visualization of occurrences in space and time
The systematic quality assessment above applies to any clade. With the pipeline established, we can now focus on a single family for the visualization work that follows. Canidae — the family containing wolves, foxes, and their extinct relatives — has a well-sampled fossil record extending back to the Eocene, making it a useful working example.
We pull the full Canidae dataset:

canids = pbdb_occurrences(
    base_name = "Canidae",
    show      = "full",
    vocab     = "pbdb",
)

The specification [:min_ma, :max_ma] => function => :mid_ma tells transform to pass both source columns together as arguments to the function, and store the result in the new column :mid_ma.

3.1 Geographic visualization
GeoMakie.jl extends the standard Makie figure/axis system with GeoAxis, a specialised axis type that understands geographic coordinates and map projections. The API is otherwise identical to a regular Axis: you place it in a Figure, then call plotting functions on it.







TipMap projections



A projection is a mathematical transformation from a spherical Earth surface onto a flat plane. No projection is distortion-free; different projections make different trade-offs between preserving area, shape, distance, and direction.
GeoAxis accepts a dest keyword that specifies the target projection using a PROJ string. "+proj=natearth2" is the Natural Earth II projection — a pseudocylindrical projection that balances area and shape distortion reasonably well for a world map. Other common choices include "+proj=moll" (Mollweide, equal-area) and "+proj=longlat" (plain longitude/latitude, no transformation).


3.1.1 Building the map

fig = Figure(size = (900, 500))

ga = GeoAxis(
    fig[1, 1];
    dest        = "+proj=natearth2",
    title       = "Fossil occurrences of Canidae",
    xlabel      = "Longitude",
    ylabel      = "Latitude",
)

## Draw land outlines as filled polygons
poly!(ga, GeoMakie.land(); color = :whitesmoke, strokecolor = :gray60, strokewidth = 0.4)

## Overlay occurrence points
scatter!(
    ga,
    canids_geo.lng,
    canids_geo.lat;
    color      = (:firebrick, 0.5),
    markersize = 5,
)

fig











TipGeoMakie.land()



GeoMakie.land() returns a GeoJSON FeatureCollection containing the outlines of Earth’s land masses from the Natural Earth dataset, which is bundled with GeoMakie. poly! knows how to render GeoJSON feature collections directly onto a GeoAxis.
The color argument for the occurrence scatter uses a tuple (:firebrick, 0.5), where the second element is the alpha (opacity) channel — values run from 0.0 (transparent) to 1.0 (fully opaque). Partial transparency is useful here because many points overlap; reducing opacity lets overlapping density show through.



3.1.2 Coloring by age
A single color for all points treats all epochs identically. We can encode the midpoint age as a color using a continuous colormap, which reveals whether canid occurrences in different parts of the world tend to be from different time periods.

fig2 = Figure(size = (900, 520))

ga2 = GeoAxis(
    fig2[1, 1];
    dest  = "+proj=natearth2",
    title = "Canidae fossil occurrences, colored by midpoint age (Ma)",
)

poly!(ga2, GeoMakie.land(); color = :whitesmoke, strokecolor = :gray60, strokewidth = 0.4)

sc = scatter!(
    ga2,
    canids_geo.lng,
    canids_geo.lat;
    color      = canids_geo.mid_ma,
    colormap   = :viridis,
    markersize = 6,
)

Colorbar(fig2[1, 2], sc; label = "Age (Ma)", flipaxis = false)

fig2











TipColorbars and the Colorbar function



When scatter! is called with a numeric color vector and a colormap, it returns a plot object that carries the mapping from data values to colors. Passing that object to Colorbar creates a legend axis showing the color scale.
fig2[1, 2] places the colorbar in column 2 of the figure grid, to the right of the map. flipaxis = false puts the colorbar labels on the left side of the bar (adjacent to the map).




3.2 Temporal visualization
The geographic map shows where canids were found; a temporal plot shows when. The temporal distribution of fossil occurrences is a central quantity in paleontology: it reflects both the evolutionary history of the group and the preservational biases of the geological record.

3.2.1 Distribution of midpoint ages
A histogram is the natural first look at the temporal distribution. The x-axis is geological age in millions of years; note that by convention, time on paleontological plots runs right to left (older on the right), so that “forward in time” means moving left.

fig3 = Figure(size = (700, 350))
ax3  = Axis(
    fig3[1, 1];
    xlabel    = "Midpoint age (Ma)",
    ylabel    = "Number of occurrences",
    title     = "Temporal distribution of Canidae fossil occurrences",
    xreversed = true,
)

hist!(ax3, canids_geo.mid_ma; bins = 40, color = (:steelblue, 0.8))

fig3











TipReversed time axis



The xreversed = true keyword on Axis reverses the direction of the x-axis so that zero (the present) is on the right and the past extends leftward. This matches the stratigraphic convention used throughout the paleontological literature, where older strata are drawn deeper (lower or further left) than younger ones.



3.2.2 Age uncertainty
Each record’s age is a range (min_ma to max_ma), not a precise date. We can visualise the spread of this uncertainty by plotting the width of each record’s age bracket:

canids_geo = transform(
    canids_geo,
    [:min_ma, :max_ma] => ((lo, hi) -> hi .- lo) => :age_range_ma
)

fig4 = Figure(size = (700, 350))
ax4  = Axis(
    fig4[1, 1];
    xlabel = "Age range width (Ma)",
    ylabel = "Number of occurrences",
    title  = "Distribution of stratigraphic age uncertainty, Canidae",
)

hist!(ax4, canids_geo.age_range_ma; bins = 40, color = (:darkorange, 0.8))

fig4




Wide age ranges reflect coarse stratigraphic resolution in the original collections. Narrow ranges indicate that the fossil was found in a well-dated stratigraphic unit. The shape of this distribution is itself informative: it reflects how well-dated different parts of the geological record are for this taxon.



3.3 Putting it together: a reusable workflow
The steps above form a complete, repeatable pipeline. Here they are collected into a compact sequence that can be adapted for any taxon:
using PaleobiologyDB, DataFrames, CairoMakie, GeoMakie

## 1. Acquire
raw = pbdb_occurrences(
    base_name = "Canidae",
    show      = "full",
    vocab     = "pbdb",
)

## 2. Validate (coordinates and age bounds required)
clean = dropmissing(raw, [:lng, :lat, :min_ma, :max_ma])

## 3. Derive midpoint age
clean = transform(
    clean,
    [:min_ma, :max_ma] => ((lo, hi) -> (lo .+ hi) ./ 2) => :mid_ma
)

## 4. Map (colored by age)
fig = Figure(size = (900, 500))
ga  = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest = "+proj=natearth2", title = "Canidae occurrences")
poly!(ga, GeoMakie.land(); color = :whitesmoke, strokecolor = :gray60, strokewidth = 0.4)
sc  = scatter!(ga, clean.lng, clean.lat; color = clean.mid_ma, colormap = :viridis, markersize = 6)
Colorbar(fig[1, 2], sc; label = "Age (Ma)", flipaxis = false)
display(fig)

## 5. Temporal histogram
fig2 = Figure(size = (700, 350))
ax   = Axis(fig2[1, 1]; xlabel = "Midpoint age (Ma)", ylabel = "Occurrences", xreversed = true)
hist!(ax, clean.mid_ma; bins = 40, color = (:steelblue, 0.8))
display(fig2)

Repeat the complete workflow above for a different carnivoran family of your choice — for example "Felidae" (cats), "Ursidae" (bears), or "Mustelidae" (weasels and kin).

How many occurrence records does the PBDB hold for your chosen family?
How many were dropped due to missing coordinates?
Does the geographic distribution of occurrences match your expectation given what you know about the group’s present-day range?
What does the temporal histogram tell you about when the fossil record of this family is densest?





Exercise 2The PBDB supports filtering by geographic bounding box using the lngmin, lngmax, latmin, and latmax parameters.

Retrieve Canidae occurrences restricted to North America (approximately lngmin = -170, lngmax = -50, latmin = 15, latmax = 75).
Retrieve Canidae occurrences restricted to Eurasia (approximately lngmin = -10, lngmax = 180, latmin = 10, latmax = 75).
Produce a single figure with two panels side by side — one histogram for each region — showing the temporal distribution of midpoint ages.
Do the two regions show different temporal patterns? What might explain any differences you observe?

Hint: To place two axes side by side, use Axis(fig[1, 1]; ...) and Axis(fig[1, 2]; ...).




Exercise 3Fossil occurrences from the PBDB come with a genus field (when show = ["class"] is requested and vocab = "pbdb" is set).

Using the groupby and combine functions from DataFrames, count the number of occurrences per genus in your cleaned Canidae dataset.
Sort the result by occurrence count in descending order.
Which five genera have the most fossil occurrences?
Produce a bar chart (use barplot! in CairoMakie) showing the top ten genera by occurrence count.

Hint: groupby(df, :genus) groups the rows; combine(gdf, nrow => :count) counts rows per group.

text:
0.1 1

0.1.1 Bayes theorem
Suppose that we have a fair coin and a biased coin that always comes up heads. We run an experiment consisting of three independent events: - we choose one of the two coins at random - we flip that coin once - and then we flip it again. Suppose that the coin we have chosen comes up heads both times. What is the probability that it is biased?
For a single toss with the coin, we know:
\(\Pr(H \mid \text{biased}) = 1.0\)
\(\Pr(H \mid \text{fair}) = 0.5\)
For two tosses with the coin, we know:
\(\Pr( HH \mid \text{biased}) = (1.0)(1.0) = 1.0\)
\(\Pr( HH \mid \text{fair}) = (0.5)(0.5) = 0.25\)
For the prior probability of the coin, we know:
\(\Pr(\text{biased}) = 0.5\)
\(\Pr(\text{fair}) = 0.5\)
So:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(\text{biased} \mid HH) &= \frac{ \Pr( HH \mid \text{biased}) \Pr(\text{biased}) }{ \left[ \Pr( HH \mid \text{biased}) \Pr(\text{biased}) \right] + \left[ \Pr( HH \mid \text{fair}) \Pr(\text{fair}) \right] } \\
    &= \frac{ 1.0 \cdot 0.5 }{ (1.0)(0.5) + (0.25)(0.5) } \\
    &= \frac{ 0.5 }{ (0.5) + (0.125) } \\
    &= 0.8
\end{aligned}
\]


0.1.2 Brute force
Sample space:
𝑆 = {(F, TT), (F, HT), (F, TH), (F, HH), (B, HH)}
\(HH\) occurs \(\frac{2}{5}\) times = \(0.8\).

2 Set up







Set up the computation environment


Create a new directory to host the project directory:
$HOME/Projects/20251201_dicegames
and, within this, generate a new Julia project, DiceGames, using the Julia package manager Pkg.
Then change into the project directory, and, making sure to invoke the correct Julia project path, add the Distributions.jl package.







Solution


$ mkdir -p ~/Projects/20251201_dicegames
$ cd ~/Projects/20251201_dicegames
$ julia -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.generate("DiceGames")'
$ cd DiceGames
$ julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.add("Distributions")'

title: (Just enough) Julia for scientific informatics, modeling, and reasoning
text:
A “die” (singular; plural is “dice”) is a device used for generating random outcomes in a finite discrete sample space. As a physical object, a die typically corresponds to some device that has a fixed, finite number of distinguishable “sides”, each of which can be mapped unambiguously, if not always uniquely, to a “face”, representing a unique and mutually-exclusive outcome in a fixed sample space . Dice are often marked with symbols to allow for identification of sides with faces. As in many modern dice the outcomes are indexed numerically, representing samples from a subset of the natural numbers, the symbols on these faces are numbers indicating integer values \({1, 2, \dots, N}\), where \(N\) is the number of faces.



A type of die most of us are familiar with today is a 6-sided die 1: 🎲. Here, the die has six sides, and each side is marked with a distinct symbol to allow it to unique represent a distinct face in the sample space 2. Today, very often, the faces are represented by a subset of the natural numbers \(\mathcal{S} \subset \mathrm{N}\), i.e., \(\mathcal{S} = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\), though other symbols have and continue to be used (e.g. …).
1 “d6” in dice notation, which we will discuss later2 Some forms of dice, especially earlier ones, had more “sides” than faces, with multiple sides marked with the same symbol


A die is “cast” 3 , “thrown”, or “rolled” to generate an outcome from its sample space, (usually) with the face on the side aligned upwards after it stops moving representing the realized outcome.
3 “Cast is the die!”, or “Iactea est alea!”, Caesar uttered when moving forward to seize Rome. Classical Latin allows either “Cast is the die!” and the “The die is cast!” as grammatically correct ways to express different emphases. I feel the common translation of “The die is cast” to conform to modern English patterns of expression misses the intended weight of Caesar’s utterance.For example, rolling a six-sided die once will result in one of the six faces, \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\), showing as the outcome.


What are the elementary outcomes of the sample space of a 6-sided die? Explicitly enumerate them, and then mathematical notation to express them more compactly.
Assuming a “fair” 6-sided die, what is the probability of each of the outcomes in the sample space?

Explicitly list all the elementary outcomes.
Write down a general mathemaIn Ltical expression for

What parametric probability distribution can we use to model this?
More generally, given a hypothetical fair die with \(N\) sides, describe the sample space, probability, and probability distribution of its outcomes.





While the six-sided cuboid die is most familiar to most people today, dice types vary in the number of sides, such as two-sided, four-sided, ten-sided, twenty-sided etc. dice, corresponding to sample spaces with corresponding varying numbers of elementary outcomes (2, 4, 10, 20, etc.)
A standard set of such six such generalized polyhedral dice types are found across a broad range of games and recreational contexts, consisting of: (1) a four-sided die, (2) a six-sided die, (3) an eight-sided die, (4) a ten-sided die, (5) a twelve-sided die, and (6) a twenty-sided die. For convenience, we may use the dice notation used by these game communities to reference specific types of these dice: d4, d6, d8, d10, d12, and d20, respectively.
In each of these dice, each of its sides maps to a unique integer from 1 to the number of sides. Thus an \(N\)-sided die can be seen as having a sample space consisting of \(\{1, 2, \dots N\}\). This mapping to natural numbers allows construction of more complex sample spaces by allowing for combining outcomes from multiple dice using natural number algebra such as addition.
Most of us are accustomed to the concept of the familiar cuboid six-sided die used in this way, e.g., when rolling two, three, or more of these and taking the total of the individual values of the roll as the outcome. A dice pool, discussed next, is a generalization of this concept.



We can model a dice pool as a multiset 4 of dice that is constructed by sampling with replacement from a set of candidate dice types. For example, there are many games in which various different moves and plays are effected by sampling from a dice pool made up of two units of single type of die (six-sided).
4 A multiset is a collection of distinguishable elements with, unlike sets, allowance for repeats.

With the distribution of each die being uniform with support (range of values over which a non-zero probability is defined) in \([1, 6]\), what is the support of the distribution of the sum of values of two six-sided dice?





We can describe the configuration of a dice pool using dice notation, which enumerates all the dice used by the mathematical conventions of indicating products (within types) and additions (across types) to combine them.









Each side of each of these dice is indexed uniquely indexed with an integer, starting from one and proceeding in sequence, ${1, 2, }, through each and every side of the dice (with some allowance for what constitutes a “side” due to the geometrical aspects of the physical manifestation of the die, e.g. a pyramid for a 4-sided die has the edges for “side” ). As such, an \(N-\)sided die, where \(N\) is some natural number greater than 1, \(N \in \mathbb{N}, N > 1\) has a sample space consisting of a subset of natural numbers, \(\mathcal{S} \subset \mathbb{N}, \mathcal{S} = \{1, 2, \dots, N\}\).

Here is a technique that will solve EVERY single probability calculation problem conceivable.
When asked what is the probability of some event,


Count all the elementary outcomes.
Count all elementary outcomes that are included in (or correspond to) the event.

Then divide the second by the first.

title: Processing data for plotting across the antimeridian with vector data
text:
using GeoMakie, CairoMakie
The antimeridian artifacts that arise when centering a projection on \(180°\) are a symptom of a more general problem: longitude values in the standard \([-180°, 180°]\) range are not continuous with respect to an arbitrary map center \(\lambda_0\). A segment whose two endpoints have longitudes of \(170°\) and \(-170°\) spans only \(20°\) of arc in reality, but their coordinate difference is \(340°\) — and the renderer, knowing nothing about spherical topology, draws a line spanning nearly the full width of the plot. The same problem arises whenever your data straddle the longitude that lies \(180°\) from \(\lambda_0\): centering on \(-100°\) (central North America) causes artifacts near \(80°\,\text{E}\), for instance.
Fixing the problem requires two distinct operations, depending on the geometry type:
crumbs: [[01-03]{.indexed-content-number} [Processing data for plotting across the antimeridian with vector data]{.indexed-content-title}]{.indexed-content-entry}

title: Processing data for plotting across the antimeridian with vector data
text:
1 Longitude normalization
The standard longitude domain \([-180°, 180°]\) is just one period of a circular quantity. For a map centered on \(\lambda_0\), the appropriate domain is \([\lambda_0 - 180°,\ \lambda_0 + 180°]\). Remapping a longitude \(\lambda\) into this domain is a single modular arithmetic operation:
\[
\lambda' = \bigl((\lambda - \lambda_0 + 180) \bmod 360\bigr) - 180 + \lambda_0
\]

"""
    normalize_lon(lon, lon_0=0.0)

Remap longitude `lon` (degrees) into the half-open interval
`[lon_0 - 180, lon_0 + 180)`, preserving its position on the circle.
"""
1normalize_lon(lon, lon_0=0.0) = mod(lon - lon_0 + 180.0, 360.0) - 180.0 + lon_0


1

mod(x, 360) returns a value in \([0°, 360°)\); subtracting \(180°\) and re-centering on lon_0 shifts this into \([\lambda_0 - 180°, \lambda_0 + 180°)\).




Main.Notebook.normalize_lon


For a vector of longitudes associated with point observations, broadcasting normalization is sufficient:

1lon_0 = 180.0
2lons_raw = [160.0, 175.0, -175.0, -160.0, -90.0]
lats_raw = [-10.0,  -5.0,   -5.0,  -10.0,  20.0]

3lons_norm = normalize_lon.(lons_raw, lon_0)

fig = Figure()
ax  = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=$(lon_0)")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
4scatter!(ax, lons_norm, lats_raw)
fig


1

Central meridian of the destination projection.

2

Raw longitudes spanning the antimeridian: without normalization, the points near \(\pm175°\) would appear on opposite sides of the map.

3

Broadcast normalize_lon over every longitude in the vector.

4

Pass the normalized longitudes to the plotting call; the axis applies only the final CRS transformation, not any wrapping correction.
crumbs: [[01-03]{.indexed-content-number} [Processing data for plotting across the antimeridian with vector data]{.indexed-content-title}]{.indexed-content-entry}

title: Processing data for plotting across the antimeridian with vector data
section: 2 Inserting NaN breaks for crossing linestrings
text:
2 Inserting NaN breaks for crossing linestrings
Point normalization alone is insufficient for linestring data: after normalization, a segment that genuinely crosses the antimeridian will still produce a nearly-\(360°\)-wide artifact, because its two endpoints end up near opposite edges of the \([\lambda_0 - 180°, \lambda_0 + 180°]\) window. The simplest fix is to detect such segments and insert a NaN coordinate pair, which Makie.lines! interprets as a break in the polyline — suppressing the offending segment entirely.

"""
    antimeridian_breaks(lons, lats; lon_0=0.0)

Normalize `lons` to `[lon_0-180, lon_0+180)` and insert `NaN` sentinel
values before any segment whose normalized endpoint gap exceeds 180°.
Returns `(lons_out, lats_out)` suitable for direct use with `lines!`.
"""
function antimeridian_breaks(lons, lats; lon_0=0.0)
1    lons_n  = normalize_lon.(lons, lon_0)
    lons_out = Float64[]
    lats_out = Float64[]
    for i in eachindex(lons_n)
        push!(lons_out, lons_n[i])
        push!(lats_out, lats[i])
2        if i < lastindex(lons_n) && abs(lons_n[i+1] - lons_n[i]) > 180.0
3            push!(lons_out, NaN)
            push!(lats_out, NaN)
        end
    end
    return lons_out, lats_out
end


1

Normalize all longitudes to the target domain before checking gaps.

2

After normalization, a gap larger than \(180°\) can only result from a genuine antimeridian crossing; identical-arc segments will have gaps \(\leq 180°\).

3

Makie.lines! treats any coordinate pair containing NaN as a discontinuity; inserting one here drops the crossing segment from the rendered polyline.




Main.Notebook.antimeridian_breaks



lon_0  = 180.0

1# Synthetic track crossing the antimeridian twice
lons_track = [150.0, 165.0, 178.0, -170.0, -155.0, -140.0]
lats_track = [ 30.0,  25.0,  18.0,    8.0,    2.0,   -5.0]

lons_fixed, lats_fixed = antimeridian_breaks(lons_track, lats_track; lon_0)

fig = Figure()
ax  = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=$(lon_0)")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
2lines!(ax, lons_fixed, lats_fixed; color=:tomato, linewidth=2)
scatter!(ax, lons_fixed, lats_fixed; color=:tomato)
fig


1

This track starts in the western Pacific, crosses \(180°\), and continues into the central Pacific — a trajectory that without correction would draw a nearly-full-width horizontal artifact.

2

The fixed coordinate arrays are passed directly; lines! handles the NaN breaks automatically.













TipNaN breaks vs. exact splitting





Inserting NaN breaks removes the crossing segment, leaving a visible gap in the polyline at the antimeridian. For most visualization purposes — species occurrence tracks, migration routes, ship or aircraft paths — this gap is acceptable and clearly communicates the map edge. For contexts where the continuity of the line matters visually (e.g., a contour line or the boundary of a species range polygon), you should instead split the geometry at the exact crossing point, as described in the next section.
crumbs: [[01-03]{.indexed-content-number} [Processing data for plotting across the antimeridian with vector data]{.indexed-content-title}]{.indexed-content-entry}

title: Processing data for plotting across the antimeridian with vector data
text:
3 Exact splitting at the antimeridian
When geometric continuity matters — for contour lines, coastlines loaded from external sources, or range polygons — you can compute the latitude at which the segment crosses \(\lambda_0 \pm 180°\) and split the segment there, inserting two correctly-terminated endpoints at the boundary. The crossing latitude follows from linear interpolation along the segment:
\[
\lambda_{\text{cross}} = \lambda_0 + 180° \cdot \operatorname{sign}(\Delta\lambda)
\] \[
\phi_{\text{cross}} = \phi_1 + (\phi_2 - \phi_1)\,\frac{\lambda_{\text{cross}} - \lambda_1}{\lambda_2 - \lambda_1}
\]
where \(\Delta\lambda = \lambda_2 - \lambda_1\) is the longitude gap after normalization, and \(\phi_1, \phi_2\) are the endpoint latitudes.

"""
    split_at_antimeridian(lons, lats; lon_0=0.0)

Split a linestring at every antimeridian crossing, returning a
`Vector` of `(lons, lats)` segment tuples, each free of crossings.
Endpoints of adjacent segments share the exact crossing latitude.
"""
function split_at_antimeridian(lons, lats; lon_0=0.0)
    lons_n   = normalize_lon.(lons, lon_0)
1    segments = Tuple{Vector{Float64}, Vector{Float64}}[]
    seg_lons = [lons_n[1]]
    seg_lats = [lats[1]]
    for i in 1:(length(lons_n) - 1)
        Δλ = lons_n[i+1] - lons_n[i]
2        if abs(Δλ) > 180.0
3            λ_cross = lon_0 + 180.0 * sign(Δλ)
            t       = (λ_cross - lons_n[i]) / Δλ
4            ϕ_cross = lats[i] + t * (lats[i+1] - lats[i])
5            push!(seg_lons, λ_cross)
            push!(seg_lats, ϕ_cross)
            push!(segments, (copy(seg_lons), copy(seg_lats)))
6            seg_lons = [λ_cross - 360.0 * sign(Δλ)]
            seg_lats = [ϕ_cross]
        end
        push!(seg_lons, lons_n[i+1])
        push!(seg_lats, lats[i+1])
    end
7    push!(segments, (seg_lons, seg_lats))
    return segments
end


1

Accumulate completed segments as a vector of (lons, lats) pairs; each returned segment is free of antimeridian crossings.

2

A normalized gap larger than \(180°\) signals a crossing, as in antimeridian_breaks.

3

The crossing longitude is at the boundary of the current window: \(\lambda_0 + 180°\) or \(\lambda_0 - 180°\) depending on direction of travel.

4

Linear interpolation along the segment gives the exact crossing latitude \(\phi_\text{cross}\).

5

Close the current segment at the crossing point and store it.

6

Open the new segment on the other side of the boundary: shift by \(\pm360°\) so the continuation is correctly positioned in the normalized window.

7

Append the final (possibly unclosed) segment after the loop.




Main.Notebook.split_at_antimeridian



lon_0    = 180.0
1segments = split_at_antimeridian(lons_track, lats_track; lon_0)

fig = Figure()
ax  = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest="+proj=eqearth +lon_0=$(lon_0)")
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax))
2for (sl, sp) in segments
    lines!(ax, sl, sp; color=:steelblue, linewidth=2)
    scatter!(ax, sl, sp; color=:steelblue)
end
fig


1

Returns a Vector of segment pairs; each segment terminates precisely at the antimeridian boundary.

2

Plot each segment independently; adjacent segments share a boundary endpoint, so the track appears visually continuous with no gap at the antimeridian.













TipPolygon data and GeometryOps.jl





For polygon geometries — species range polygons, biome boundaries, ocean basins — antimeridian splitting is considerably more involved: a polygon that crosses the boundary must be cut into two closed polygons, each with a shared edge running along the antimeridian. Implementing this correctly requires handling winding order, hole geometries, and coordinate ring closure.
Rather than implementing this manually, use GeometryOps.jl, which provides a fix function with an antimeridian_correction pass that handles both linestring and polygon geometries via GeoInterface.jl-compatible objects:
using GeometryOps, GeoInterface

geom_fixed = GeometryOps.fix(geom; corrections=[GeometryOps.AntimeridianCorrection()])
The corrected geometry can then be passed directly to poly! or lines! on a GeoAxis without further coordinate manipulation.

section: 2 Geospatial data types: vector vs. raster
text:
2 Geospatial data types: vector vs. raster

Proficiencies

Distinguish vector and raster as the two fundamental models for representing geographic information.
Identify which data model is appropriate for a given biological or environmental dataset.



Geographical feature data can be computationally modeled in either vector or raster form.
Vector data models the world as a collection of discrete geometrical objects (lines, polygons, and points).
Raster data models the world as a grid of cells, each associated with a value defined over its spatial support.









Vector
Raster




Represents
Discrete objects with defined location or boundary
Continuous surfaces sampled on a regular grid


Geometry
Points, lines, polygons
Grid of equally-sized cells (pixels)


Common formats
Shapefile (.shp), GeoPackage (.gpkg), GeoJSON (.geojson)
GeoTIFF (.tif), NetCDF (.nc), ASCII Grid (.asc)


Julia tooling
GeoDataFrames.jl, Shapefile.jl, GeoJSON.jl
Rasters.jl, ArchGDAL.jl


Typical biological sources
GBIF occurrences, IUCN range polygons, Natural Earth base layers, PBDB fossil localities
BIOCLIM/WorldClim climate layers, PALEOCLIM, SRTM elevation, SDM output surfaces


Plot function on GeoAxis
scatter!, lines!, poly!
heatmap!, surface!


Resolution concept
Spatial precision of coordinates
Cell size (e.g. 2.5 arcminutes, 1 km)


Missing data
Absent rows or missing attribute values
NaN cells or a defined NoData value









NoteMesh representations



We might also encounter spatial or geographic features modeled as a mesh. In computational geometry and scientific computing, spatial data are often represented as meshes: collections of vertices and connected cells (edges, faces, or volumes) with explicit topology. Vector geometries correspond to low-dimensional meshes (e.g., points, polylines, polygonal faces), while raster data correspond to structured meshes (regular grids). Mesh representations generalize both models. However, while vector geometries and raster are classical GIS data models, “mesh” is a geometric and topological data representation used for discretizing spatial domains.

3 Working with vector data

Proficiencies

Select the appropriate Makie plot function for each geometry type.
Control color, stroke, and transparency for geographic layers.



Geographic vector data are plotted with a different Makie plot function depending on their geometry type: lines (an ordered sequence of coordinate pairs), polygons (a closed bounded region), or points (a single coordinate pair) being plotted by lines!. poly!, and scatter!, respectively.








Geometry type
Plot function
Typical biological source




Point
scatter!
Occurrence records, fossil localities, sampling stations


Line / polyline
lines!
Coastlines, rivers, transects


Polygon
poly!
Land masks, country/state borders, biome boundaries, species ranges




3.1 Plotting NaturalEarth geometry data
The NaturalEarth.jl package provides pre-cleaned Natural Earth datasets as GeoDataFrame objects and is the standard source for background geometry in GeoMakie workflows. The geometry property of the these objects provides the plotting data required.


3.2 Lines
Line vector datasets are plotted using lines!. An example of this is the dataset returned by the GeoMakie.coastlines() function, which is the NaturalEarth 110m scale coastline line vector dataset.

using CairoMakie, GeoMakie, NaturalEarth

1coasts = naturalearth("coastline", 110)

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest = "+proj=eqearth")
2lines!(ax, coasts.geometry; color = :black, linewidth = 0.5)
fig


1

Load the NaturalEarth 110 meter scale coastline dataset.

2

Pass its geometry property to the lines! function as data to plot.









3.3 Polygons
poly! draws filled closed regions. The color keyword controls the fill; strokecolor and strokewidth control the border. Passing a color as an (name, alpha) tuple sets transparency.

using CairoMakie, GeoMakie, NaturalEarth

land = naturalearth("land", 110)

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1]; dest = "+proj=eqearth")
poly!(ax, land.geometry;
    color       = :lightgray,
    strokecolor = :black,
    strokewidth = 0.3)
fig






3.4 Points
scatter! draws individual coordinate pairs as markers. Here a small set of locations is specified manually; in later chapters, occurrence records from GBIF and fossil localities from PBDB will be passed in directly from data frames.

cities = [
    (114.17,  22.32),   # Hong Kong
    (103.82,   1.35),   # Singapore
    (106.84,  -6.21),   # Jakarta
]
lons = first.(cities)
lats = last.(cities)

fig = Figure()
ax = GeoAxis(fig[1, 1];
    dest   = "+proj=longlat",
    limits = (95, 125, -15, 30))
poly!(ax, land.geometry; color = :lightgray, strokewidth = 0)
lines!(ax, GeoMakie.coastlines(ax); color = :black, linewidth = 0.5)
scatter!(ax, lons, lats; color = :firebrick, markersize = 10)
fig

Installs, selects, updates, and removes Julia versions.
juliaup status or juliaup update



For ordinary use, the distinction is simple: use julia to run Julia, and use juliaup to manage the Julia installation.


The Julia project recommends installing the latest stable release through juliaup. The stable release is represented by the release channel. When that channel is updated, juliaup installs the newest stable patch release without requiring a new installation procedure.







TipUse the stable release



Use the release channel for this course unless an exercise specifies another version. The lts channel provides the long-term support release, while beta, rc, and nightly provide prerelease or development versions. Prerelease versions are intended for testing Julia itself and may not work with every package used in the course.

If Julia was installed previously by another method, first identify the version and executable that the shell currently finds:
$ julia --version
$ which julia
In PowerShell, use:
PS> julia --version
PS> Get-Command julia
An older installation can coexist with juliaup, but 2 different julia commands on the PATH make it unclear which installation will start. The juliaup documentation recommends removing earlier Julia installations and their manually added PATH entries before installing through juliaup. Use the earlier installation’s documented uninstaller, or ask for assistance if the computer is managed by an institution.



Open Windows Terminal, PowerShell, or Command Prompt. Install Julia from the Microsoft Store source with winget:
PS> winget install --name Julia --id 9NJNWW8PVKMN -e -s msstore
This installs juliaup and the current stable Julia release. When installation finishes, close the terminal and open a new one so that the new shell receives the updated PATH.
If winget or the Microsoft Store is unavailable, open the official Julia installation page and use its MSIX App Installer option. On a managed computer, installation may be restricted by institutional policy; in that case, contact the system administrator rather than substituting an unofficial download.







NoteWindows Start menu and terminal access



The Windows installation also provides a Start menu entry and a Windows Terminal profile. This course uses the julia shell command because the same command works on Windows, macOS, and Linux and makes the selected Julia version explicit.




Open a terminal and run the installer command published by the Julia project:
$ curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh
The command downloads the installer from install.julialang.org and passes it to the shell. Read the displayed installation summary, accept the defaults, and allow the installer to add Julia to the PATH. The default installation belongs to the current user and normally does not require sudo or administrator access.
When installation finishes, close the terminal and open a new one. This starts a new shell that reads the configuration updated by the installer. If the installer prints a different command for refreshing the current shell, that command can be used instead.






ImportantRun installers only from the official domain



The command above executes code downloaded from the network. Type it only after confirming that the address is exactly https://install.julialang.org, or copy the current command from the official Julia installation page.


Do not install the Julia runtime from a Linux distribution’s package repository for this course. Distribution packages can be older than the supported Julia release or can differ from the official binaries. Use juliaup, or use an official manual binary when juliaup is not available.



Open a new shell and ask Julia to report its version:
$ julia --version
julia version 1.12.7
The exact version changes as Julia releases are published. The important result is a version line rather than a command not found error.
Next, inspect the version selected by juliaup:
$ juliaup status
The status output lists installed channels, their Julia versions, and the default channel. For a new course installation, release should be installed and selected as the default.
Confirm which executable the shell found:
$ which julia
In PowerShell, use:
PS> Get-Command julia
Finally, start Julia:
$ julia
At the julia> prompt, evaluate a small expression and inspect the runtime:
julia> 2 + 2
4

julia> VERSION
v"1.12.7"

julia> Sys.KERNEL
:Linux

julia> Sys.ARCH
:x86_64

julia> exit()
Sys.KERNEL and Sys.ARCH report the operating system kernel and processor architecture. Their values will differ on Windows, macOS, and computers with ARM processors. The final call, exit(), ends Julia and returns to the shell. The next lesson examines this interactive julia> prompt, called the Julia read-eval-print loop (REPL), in detail.



A juliaup channel is a named pointer to a Julia release or series of releases. The channel determines which runtime the julia launcher starts.








Channel form
Meaning
Example launch command




release
Latest stable Julia release.
julia +release


lts
Latest long-term support release.
julia +lts


1.12
Latest installed patch release in the Julia 1.12 series.
julia +1.12


1.12.7
One exact Julia release.
julia +1.12.7

$ juliaup add lts
$ julia +lts --version

Or update only the stable channel with:

Updating Julia and updating Julia packages are separate operations. juliaup update updates Julia runtimes. Julia’s package manager updates packages inside an environment, as described later in this chapter.



juliaup is the standard installation path, but some managed, offline, or unusual systems cannot use it. The Julia project provides manual downloads of official binaries for those cases.
A manual installation requires more decisions:

selecting the correct operating system and processor architecture
placing or unpacking the downloaded application
adding its bin directory to the shell PATH
downloading and installing later Julia releases manually

Use a manual binary only when juliaup is unavailable or a specific deployment requires it. Follow the official platform-specific instructions rather than instructions for an unofficial package or mirror.
Installing Julia does not install external Julia packages such as DataFrames or CairoMakie. Those packages belong to Julia environments and are installed by Julia’s package manager. The later lesson on environments, projects, and package management introduces that process.











Symptom
Likely cause
First check




julia: command not found or “julia is not recognized”
The current shell has not read the updated PATH, or installation did not finish.
Close every terminal window, open a new one, and run julia --version.


juliaup works but julia does not
The Julia launcher directory is not available on PATH.
Reopen the shell, then review the final message printed by the installer.


julia --version reports an unexpected older release
Another Julia executable appears earlier on PATH.
Run which julia on macOS/Linux or Get-Command julia -All in PowerShell.


winget cannot access the Store source
The Microsoft Store is disabled, unavailable, or blocked by policy.
Use the official MSIX App Installer link or contact the system administrator.


The macOS/Linux installer cannot download Julia
The network, proxy, or firewall blocks an official Julia domain.
Confirm network access to julialang.org and julialang-s3.julialang.org.


Julia starts, but the first package operation takes a long time
Packages and compiled caches are being downloaded or generated.
Let the operation finish; this is separate from installing the runtime.


VS Code cannot find Julia
VS Code was already running when Julia changed the PATH, or the Julia extension is not installed.
Restart VS Code, then confirm julia --version in its integrated terminal.



Do not repeatedly install Julia through different methods to solve a PATH problem. First locate the executable selected by the shell, then correct or remove the conflicting installation.




Exercise 1
Verify the Julia installation from a new shell.

Run julia --version and record the version.
Run juliaup status and identify the default channel.
Run which julia on macOS/Linux or Get-Command julia in PowerShell and record the executable path.
Explain the different information returned by these 3 commands.




Exercise 2Start Julia with julia. At the julia> prompt:

Evaluate 6 * 7.
Evaluate VERSION.
Evaluate Sys.KERNEL and Sys.ARCH.
End the Julia process with exit().

Identify which lines are shell commands, which lines are Julia expressions, and which lines are output.
